questions.q: Gametogenesis begins with the primordial germ cell (PGC), which is embryologically derived from:
questions.exp: Primordial germ cells are derived from the epiblast and ectoderm. (Book p265)

questions.q: Primordial germ cells are described as bipotent because they possess the developmental capability to form:
opts: All three embryonic germ layers only
questions.exp: PGCs are bipotent cells that can differentiate into either spermatogonia or oogonia. (Book p265)

questions.q: Sexual differentiation of the primordial germ cells into male or female gametogonia is fundamentally determined by the:
questions.exp: Differentiation is determined by the SRY gene (sex-related gene on chromosome Y). (Book p265)

questions.q: The SRY gene is anatomically situated on which specific chromosomal locus?
opts: Distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y
questions.exp: The SRY gene is located on the distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y. (Book p265)

questions.q: When the SRY gene on chromosome Y is absent, primordial germ cells normally differentiate into:
questions.exp: When the SRY gene is absent, PGCs differentiate into oogonia. (Book p265)

questions.q: Match the following germ-cell milestones with the time they occur — 1) Spermatogenesis first begins 2) Oogenesis first begins 3) Primordial germ cells reach the genital ridge … A) Puberty B) Intrauterine life C) 5th-6th week of gestation
questions.exp: Spermatogenesis starts only at puberty, oogenesis starts in intrauterine life, and PGCs migrate to the genital ridge by the 5th-6th week. (Book p265)

questions.q: At what stage of human development does spermatogenesis normally begin?
questions.exp: Spermatogenesis begins at puberty, unlike oogenesis which starts in intrauterine life. (Book p265)

questions.q: In the male germ cell lineage, which spermatogonial subtype divides by mitosis to replenish the stem cell reservoir?
questions.exp: Type A spermatogonia divide and replenish the stem stores of spermatogonia. (Book p265)

questions.q: The male germ cells that undergo maturation and enter spermatogenesis are designated as:
questions.exp: Type B (pale) spermatogonia undergo spermatogenesis to form primary spermatocytes. (Book p265)

questions.q: Through sequential mitotic amplification, one spermatogonium gives rise to how many primary spermatocytes?
questions.exp: One spermatogonium produces 16 primary spermatocytes. (Book p265)

questions.q: During Meiosis I of spermatogenesis, chromosome reduction occurs when one primary spermatocyte (46, XY) divides to form:
opts: Two secondary spermatocytes (23, X and 23, Y)
One secondary spermatocyte and one polar body
questions.exp: In Meiosis I, chromosome number is halved, yielding two secondary spermatocytes (23, X and 23, Y) from each primary spermatocyte. (Book p265)

questions.q: How many haploid spermatids are produced from a single primary spermatocyte and from a single spermatogonium, respectively?
questions.exp: Each primary spermatocyte produces 4 spermatids, and one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids. (Book p265)

questions.q: The developmental process termed spermiogenesis is best defined as the:
opts: Morphological transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa without cell division
First meiotic division reducing chromosome number to haploid
Second meiotic division producing round spermatids
Release of mature spermatozoa into the tubule lumen
questions.exp: Spermiogenesis is the morphological transformation of round spermatids into spermatozoa without meiosis or mitosis. (Book p265)

questions.q: The process by which mature spermatozoa detach from Sertoli cells and are released into the seminiferous tubule lumen is termed:
questions.exp: Spermiation is the process of release of sperm into the lumen of the seminiferous tubules. (Book p265)

questions.q: What is the total duration required for the complete cycle of spermatogenesis in human testes?
questions.exp: The time taken for spermatogenesis is 70–74 days (~72 days). (Book p265)

questions.q: The time required specifically for the morphogenetic phase of spermiogenesis is:
questions.exp: The time taken for spermiogenesis is 10–14 days. (Book p265)

questions.q: Fill up: A full cycle of spermatogenesis takes ______ days, of which the morphogenetic phase of spermiogenesis alone occupies ______ days.
questions.exp: Spermatogenesis takes 70-74 days (~72 days) and spermiogenesis alone takes 10-14 days. (Book p265)

questions.q: In the seminiferous tubule, which germ cells are normally housed within the basal compartment beneath the blood-testis barrier?
questions.exp: The basal compartment contains spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes; adluminal holds secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperms. (Book p266)

questions.q: Which germ cell populations reside in the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous tubule, positioned luminal to the blood-testis barrier?
opts: Primordial germ cells and Leydig interstitial cells
Only Type A and Type B spermatogonia
questions.exp: The adluminal compartment contains secondary spermatocytes, spermatids, and sperms, while the basal compartment contains spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes. (Book p266)

questions.q: The blood-testis barrier that physically partitions the seminiferous tubule into basal and adluminal compartments is formed by specialized tight junctions between:
questions.exp: Specialized tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli sustentacular cells establish the blood-testis barrier, dividing the seminiferous epithelium into basal and adluminal compartments. (Book p266)

questions.q: During spermiogenesis, the acrosomal cap of the sperm head is derived from which cytoplasmic organelle of the spermatid?
questions.exp: The acrosomal cap is formed by the Golgi apparatus of the spermatid. (Book p266)

questions.q: The middle piece of the mature spermatozoon is termed the powerhouse of the cell because it is composed of condensed:
questions.exp: Mitochondria aggregate in the middle piece, serving as the powerhouse of the sperm. (Book p266)

questions.q: The axial filament forming the flagellar tail of the mature spermatozoon originates from the spermatid's:
questions.exp: The axial filament/tail is formed by the centriole. (Book p266)

questions.q: The axoneme within the flagellar tail of the spermatozoon exhibits which characteristic microtubular arrangement?
questions.exp: The tail of the sperm has a characteristic 9+2 arrangement of microtubules. (Book p266)

questions.q: What is the total overall length of a normal mature human spermatozoon?
questions.exp: The total size of a mature spermatozoon is 50–60 µm (compared to 120 µm for an ovum). (Book p266)

questions.q: What is the normal fertilisable lifespan of human spermatozoa within the female genital tract?
questions.exp: The fertilisable lifespan of sperm is 48–72 hours, whereas the ovum's lifespan is 12–24 hours. (Book p266)

questions.q: In the male reproductive tract, spermatozoa attain structural maturity in the proximal epididymis, while progressive forward motility is acquired in the:
questions.exp: Sperm maturity is attained in the proximal epididymis, while motility is attained in the distal epididymis. (Book p266)

questions.q: What is the time required for spermatozoa to complete transit and physiological maturation through the epididymis?
questions.exp: Epididymal maturation takes 12–14 days. (Book p266)

questions.q: The total duration required to produce fully mature, motile spermatozoa (testicular spermatogenesis plus epididymal maturation) is:
questions.exp: Total time taken to form mature sperm (spermatogenesis + epididymal maturation) is ~90 days. (Book p266)

questions.q: Following ejaculation into the vagina, how long does it take for spermatozoa to reach the fertilization site in the fallopian tube?
questions.exp: Time taken by sperm to reach the fertilization site after ejaculation is 30 minutes. (Book p266)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about human spermatozoa is TRUE?
opts: Sperm acquire progressive motility only during epididymal transit, not in the testis
Sperm gain the ability to fertilise an oocyte while still inside the seminiferous tubules
Ejaculated sperm are immediately capable of fertilising an oocyte without further change
Spermatozoa normally remain motile in the female genital tract for barely two to three hours
questions.exp: Motility is acquired during epididymal transit; fertilising capacity requires capacitation in the female tract, and sperm survive there for days. (Book p266)

questions.q: Unlike spermatogenesis which begins at puberty, oogenesis in the female commences during:
questions.exp: Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life, with oogonia entering meiosis before birth. (Book p266)

questions.q: In the fetal ovary, primary oocytes enter Meiosis I and remain arrested until puberty at which specific stage?
questions.exp: Primary oocytes arrest in the diplotene stage of prophase I, also known as the dictyate state. (Book p266)

questions.q: The prolonged resting phase of primary oocytes in the human ovary is specifically designated as the:
questions.exp: The arrested primary oocyte resting phase is called the dictyate state (absent in spermatogenesis). (Book p266)

questions.q: A primordial follicle is formed when follicular cells encircle a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I. Clinically, tests of ovarian reserve (such as AMH and antral follicle count) evaluate:
opts: The presence of an adequate pool/reservoir of resting follicles within the ovary
The mitotic division rate of granulosa cells within preantral follicles
The functional competence of the meiotic spindle in metaphase II
The rate of follicular fluid accumulation within the Graafian antrum
questions.exp: The ovary functions as a biological reservoir of follicles; ovarian reserve tests check for the presence of an adequate number of resting primordial follicles. (Book p266)

questions.q: At puberty, the resumption of Meiosis I in the preovulatory Graafian follicle is directly triggered by the:
questions.exp: Meiosis I resumes due to the preovulatory LH surge (hormone dependent). (Book p266)

questions.q: Completion of Meiosis I just prior to ovulation results in the transition from a primary oocyte into a:
opts: Secondary oocyte and first polar body
Mature ovum and second polar body
questions.exp: Ovulation marks the transition from primary oocyte to secondary oocyte along with the extrusion of the 1st polar body. (Book p266)

questions.q: The ovulated secondary oocyte promptly initiates Meiosis II but is arrested at which stage until fertilization?
questions.exp: The secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II until fertilisation occurs. (Book p266)

questions.q: What physiological event triggers the secondary oocyte to resume and complete Meiosis II?
questions.exp: Meiosis II resumes and finishes at fertilization, giving the female pronucleus and 2nd polar body. (Book p266)

questions.q: Match the germ-cell population with its number — 1) Oogonia at 20 weeks' gestation 2) Oocytes at birth 3) Oocytes at puberty … A) ~7 million B) 1-2 million C) 300,000-400,000
questions.exp: Peak oogonial number is ~7 million at 20 weeks, falling to 1-2 million at birth and 300,000-400,000 by puberty. (Book p266)

questions.q: In contrast to spermatogenesis where one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids, each oogonium ultimately gives rise to:
opts: One mature ovum and three non-functional polar bodies
Four mature ova, all of them fertilisable
Sixteen mature ova, all of them fertilisable
Sixty-four mature ova, all of them fertilisable
questions.exp: Unlike spermatogenesis, where one spermatogonium yields 64 spermatids, each oogonium ultimately gives rise to a single mature ovum (female pronucleus) plus non-functional polar bodies. (Book p267)

questions.q: What is the average diameter of a mature, ovulated human ovum?
questions.exp: The size of a mature human ovum is 120 µm. (Book p267)

questions.q: What is the fertilisable lifespan of a freshly ovulated human secondary oocyte?
questions.exp: The fertilisable lifespan of an ovum is 12–24 hours. (Book p267)

questions.q: On transvaginal ultrasound, what is the expected diameter of a mature Graafian follicle immediately prior to ovulation?
questions.exp: The size of the mature preovulatory follicle just before ovulation is 18–20 mm. (Book p267)

questions.q: Primordial follicle formation in the human female fetus begins at 14 weeks and is fully complete by:
questions.exp: Follicle formation begins at 14 weeks and is completed by 22–24 weeks of intrauterine life. (Book p267)

questions.q: The total number of germ cells/follicles in the female ovary reaches its lifetime peak of 6–7 million at:
questions.exp: The maximum peak of 6–7 million follicles occurs at the 5th month of intrauterine life. (Book p267)

questions.q: At birth, the total follicular endowment present in both ovaries has declined by atresia to approximately:
questions.exp: At birth, the number of follicles in the ovary drops to 1–2 million. (Book p267)

questions.q: By the time a female reaches puberty, the ovarian follicular reserve has further diminished to:
opts: 10,000, that is ten thousand follicles only
questions.exp: By puberty the ovarian follicular pool is further reduced to 4-5 lakh (400,000-500,000) follicles. (Book p267)

questions.q: During the active reproductive years, approximately how many ovarian follicles undergo atresia every month?
questions.exp: Every month, roughly 1000 follicles undergo atresia while normally only one reaches ovulation. (Book p267)

questions.q: At the onset of menopause, the number of functional primordial follicles remaining in the ovary is:
questions.exp: At menopause, there are virtually no follicles remaining in the ovary. (Book p267)

questions.q: Primordial germ cells are classified as pluripotent because they have the developmental potential to:
opts: Form all three embryonic germ layers
Form both embryonic and extraembryonic placental tissues
Differentiate only into gonadal stromal cells
questions.exp: Germ cells are pluripotent, meaning they have the ability to form all 3 germ layers. (Book p267)

questions.q: The human zygote up to the 8-cell stage is totipotent, which signifies its unique ability to:
opts: Form both embryonic and extraembryonic tissues
Form only the three definitive embryonic germ layers
Differentiate solely into the central nervous system
Form the placenta without an embryo
questions.exp: A zygote up to the 8-cell stage is totipotent, capable of forming both embryonic and extraembryonic tissue. (Book p267)

questions.q: What is the correct sequential migratory route taken by primordial germ cells during early embryonic development?
opts: Epiblast → Yolk sac wall → Genital ridge → Gonads
Neural crest → Hypoblast → Genital ridge → Gonads
Dorsal aorta → Mesonephros → Yolk sac → Gonads
questions.exp: PGCs migrate from the epiblast to the yolk sac wall, then to the genital ridge where gonads develop. (Book p267)

questions.q: Failure of primordial germ cell migration or their aberrant arrest along the midline migratory path leads to the development of:
questions.exp: Failure of PGC migration (aberrant location) results in the formation of teratomas. (Book p267)

questions.q: Fill up: A teratoma shows tissue from all three embryonic layers, so its cell of origin behaves as a ______ cell, whereas a normal primordial germ cell is only ______.
questions.exp: Teratomas reveal the totipotent potential of germ cells, while normal PGCs are bipotent — able to form spermatogonia or oogonia only. (Book p267)

questions.q: Capacitation of spermatozoa is best defined as the physiological process by which:
opts: Sperms become capable of fertilizing the ovum
Spermatids shed excess cytoplasm to form flagella
Spermatozoa acquire progressive motility in the epididymis
Sperm heads fuse with the second polar body
questions.exp: Capacitation is the process by which sperms become capable of fertilizing the ova. (Book p268)

questions.q: In vivo capacitation takes place in the female reproductive tract over approximately how many hours?
questions.exp: In vivo capacitation takes 6–8 hours (compared to 2 hours for in vitro capacitation). (Book p268)

questions.q: Where does physiological sperm capacitation initiate, and what is its primary anatomical site of completion?
opts: Begins in the cervix; main site is the fallopian tube
Begins in the vagina; main site is the uterine cavity
Begins in the epididymis; main site is the ampulla
Begins in the vas deferens; main site is the cervix
questions.exp: Capacitation begins at the cervix, but its main site of completion is the fallopian tube. (Book p268)

questions.q: When performed in an assisted reproduction laboratory, the time required for in vitro capacitation of sperm is approximately:
questions.exp: In vitro capacitation takes approximately 2 hours. (Book p268)

questions.q: Spermatozoa attain baseline motility in the distal epididymis, but hypermotility is achieved specifically within the:
questions.exp: Motility is acquired in the distal epididymis, whereas hypermotility is attained in the female reproductive tract. (Book p268)

questions.q: During fertilization, the capacitated sperm head binds specifically to which glycoprotein receptor on the zona pellucida?
questions.exp: The zona pellucida contains specific receptors for the sperm head known as ZP3 receptors. (Book p268)

questions.q: The acrosomal reaction releases which key hydrolytic enzyme to digest a path through the zona pellucida?
questions.exp: The acrosome reaction releases enzymes including hyaluronidase to digest the zona pellucida. (Book p268)

questions.q: Following sperm-oolemma fusion, the secondary oocyte completes Meiosis II and its cortical granules exocytose what into the perivitelline space?
questions.exp: Cortical granules in the secondary oocyte cytoplasm release Ca2+ and enzymes to trigger the zona reaction. (Book p268)

questions.q: Hardening and biochemical alteration of the zona pellucida to prevent polyspermy is mediated by the combined:
questions.exp: Polyspermy is prevented by the cortical reaction and subsequent zona reaction (hardening of zona pellucida). (Book p268)

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman's oocytes fail to fertilise in vitro until albumin is added to the culture medium; albumin acts as a sterol acceptor and strips cholesterol from the sperm membrane. Which step was being reproduced?
opts: Capacitation — removal of cholesterol and seminal glycoproteins from the sperm membrane
Acrosome reaction — release of acrosin and hyaluronidase from the acrosomal cap
Cortical reaction — enzyme release that hardens the zona pellucida around the oocyte
Spermiation — detachment of mature spermatozoa from recesses in the Sertoli cell
questions.exp: Capacitation is cholesterol and glycoprotein removal from the sperm membrane (reproduced in vitro by albumin), and it must precede the acrosome reaction. (Book p268)

questions.q: Under normal physiological conditions, fertilization of the secondary oocyte occurs in the:
questions.exp: Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. (Book p269)

questions.q: In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, the day of fertilization corresponds to which cycle day?
questions.exp: Day of fertilization equals the day of ovulation, which is Day 14 in a standard 28-day cycle. (Book p269)

questions.q: The first mitotic cleavage division of the unicellular diploid zygote to form a 2-cell embryo occurs at approximately:
questions.exp: The 2-cell zygote stage is reached 30 hours after fertilization. (Book p269)

questions.q: The developing conceptus typically enters the uterine cavity at which developmental stage?
questions.exp: The 16-cell morula enters the uterine cavity from the fallopian tube. (Book p269)

questions.q: Transport of the dividing morula through the fallopian tube towards the uterine cavity is driven by:
opts: Tubal peristalsis and beating of ciliated columnar epithelial cells
Active flagellar motility of the blastomeres
questions.exp: The morula is propelled by tubal peristalsis and ciliary movement of the ciliated columnar lining. (Book p269)

questions.q: The dividing embryo resides in the fallopian tube for 3 days nourished by secretory peg cells, entering the uterus on:
questions.exp: The 16-cell morula enters the uterine cavity on the 4th day after fertilization (Day 18 of the cycle). (Book p269)

questions.q: Zona hatching, the shedding of the acellular zona pellucida to allow fluid influx and blastocyst expansion, occurs on:
questions.exp: On the 5th day after fertilization, the zona pellucida is lost (zona hatching) and fluid enters to form a blastocyst. (Book p269)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions increases the risk of tubal ectopic pregnancy by impairing normal tubal ciliary motility or peristalsis?
opts: Kartagener syndrome and progestin-only contraceptive pills
Combined oral contraceptives with high estrogen
questions.exp: Kartagener syndrome (immotile cilia) and progestin-only pills (smooth muscle relaxation) impair tubal transport, predisposing to ectopic pregnancy. (Book p269)

questions.q: Fill up: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ______ of the fallopian tube and the zygote reaches the uterine cavity about ______ days later.
questions.exp: Fertilisation occurs in the ampulla and the conceptus takes roughly 3-4 days of tubal transport to reach the uterine cavity. (Book p269)

questions.q: On which day after fertilization does normal blastocyst implantation into the endometrium initiate?
questions.exp: Implantation occurs on Day 6 after fertilization, which corresponds to Day 20 of the menstrual cycle. (Book p270)

questions.q: The receptive endometrial window during which the uterine lining is optimal for blastocyst attachment spans:
opts: Day 20 to Day 24 of the menstrual cycle
Day 10 to Day 14 of the menstrual cycle
Day 25 to Day 28 of the menstrual cycle
Day 14 to Day 18 of the menstrual cycle
questions.exp: The implantation window is Day 20 to Day 24 of the cycle, when the endometrium is maximally receptive. (Book p270)

questions.q: Slight, painless vaginal spotting occurring around cycle day 20–22 due to blastocyst burrowing into the endometrium is termed the:
opts: Hartmann sign, also called the placental sign
Palmer sign of regular uterine pulsation
questions.exp: Slight painless spotting around cycle day 20-22 from blastocyst burrowing into the endometrium is the Hartmann sign (placental sign). (Book p270)

questions.q: On early obstetric ultrasound, the very first sonographic sign confirming an intrauterine pregnancy is the:
questions.exp: The intradecidual sign (gestational sac deep inside the thickened endometrium) is the first sign seen on ultrasound. (Book p270)

questions.q: Match the correct molecular mediator with the respective stage of blastocyst implantation:
opts: Apposition: Selectin; Adhesion: Integrin; Penetration: Matrix metalloproteinases
Apposition: Integrin; Adhesion: Selectin; Penetration: Hyaluronidase
Apposition: Collagenase; Adhesion: Cadherin; Penetration: Selectin
Apposition: MMPs; Adhesion: Fibrinogen; Penetration: Integrin
questions.exp: Apposition is mediated by selectins, adhesion by integrins (most important), and penetration by matrix metalloproteinases. (Book p270)

questions.q: Following implantation, the endometrium beneath the blastocyst that will directly form the maternal component of the placenta is the:
questions.exp: Decidua basalis lies directly beneath the conceptus and forms the maternal side of the placenta. (Book p270)

questions.q: The layer of decidua that arches over and encapsulates the expanding blastocyst, separating it from the uterine cavity, is the:
questions.exp: Decidua capsularis overlies the blastocyst and separates it from the remaining uterine cavity. (Book p270)

questions.q: Match the implantation landmark with its post-ovulation timing — 1) Blastocyst enters the uterine cavity 2) Blastocyst attaches to the endometrium 3) Implantation is completed … A) Day 3-4 B) Day 6-7 C) Day 11-12
questions.exp: The blastocyst enters the cavity on day 3-4, attaches on day 6-7 and implantation is complete by day 11-12. (Book p270)

questions.q: On ultrasound examination, the double decidual sac sign is formed by the concentric echogenic rings of which two layers?
questions.exp: The double decidual sac sign is formed by the decidua capsularis and decidua parietalis. (Book p271)

questions.q: Obliteration of the uterine cavity occurs when the decidua capsularis fuses completely with the decidua parietalis at:
questions.exp: Decidua capsularis fuses with decidua parietalis, obliterating the uterine cavity at 14–16 weeks of pregnancy. (Book p271)

questions.q: Fertilization of two ova released in two different menstrual cycles by two separate acts of coitus is termed superfetation, which in humans is:
opts: Not seen, but theoretically possible only until 14–16 weeks
A common mechanism for dizygotic twins
questions.exp: Superfetation is not seen in humans; theoretically it could only occur before cavity obliteration at 14–16 weeks. (Book p271)

questions.q: Under the influence of progesterone, endometrial thickness increases to 10–12 mm primarily as a consequence of:
opts: Exudation of fibrinoid material into the glands
questions.exp: Progesterone causes marked stromal edema (most important histological finding), increasing endometrial thickness to 10–12 mm. (Book p271)

questions.q: On day 8 after fertilization, the blastocyst differentiates into which two primary structural components?
opts: Inner cell mass (embryoblast) and outer trophoblast
questions.exp: On Day 8 after fertilization, the blastocyst segregates into inner cell mass (embryoblast) and trophoblast. (Book p272)

questions.q: All three definitive embryonic germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm) and the embryo proper are derived from the:
questions.exp: The embryo proper and all 3 germ layers are formed entirely from the inner cell mass. (Book p272)

questions.q: The syncytiotrophoblast is clinically characterized as the 'hormone factory' of the placenta because it synthesizes:
opts: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and human placental lactogen (hPL)
questions.exp: The syncytiotrophoblast functions as the hormone factory of the placenta, synthesizing peptide hormones like hCG and hPL. (Book p272)

questions.q: Which population of trophoblastic cells invades maternal spiral arterioles to establish low resistance and prevent pregnancy-induced hypertension (PIH)?
questions.exp: Extravillous trophoblasts invade maternal spiral arteries, transforming them into dilated low-resistance conduits and preventing PIH. (Book p272)

questions.q: The villous trophoblast adjacent to the decidua basalis proliferates into bushy, villous projections termed the:
questions.exp: Villous trophoblast near the decidua basalis forms the chorion frondosum, which becomes the fetal side of the placenta. (Book p272)

questions.q: The smooth, non-villous portion of the trophoblast that surrounds the remaining conceptus is termed:
opts: Chorion laeve, which becomes the chorionic part of the fetal membranes
Chorion frondosum, where the villi persist and form the definitive placenta
The Nitabuch layer, where maternal and fetal tissues meet and mix
Decidua vera, the maternal lining away from the implantation site
questions.exp: Villi regress over the abembryonic pole giving chorion laeve; opposite the implantation site they persist as chorion frondosum. (Book p272)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about trophoblast differentiation is TRUE?
opts: Syncytiotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer that secretes hCG and invades the endometrium
Cytotrophoblast is the outer multinucleated layer and is the main source of hCG secretion
Syncytiotrophoblast forms by fusion of decidual stromal cells around the implanting blastocyst
Cytotrophoblast alone erodes maternal sinusoids, since it is the invasive layer in the first trimester
questions.exp: Cytotrophoblast is the inner mononuclear stem layer; syncytiotrophoblast is outer, multinucleated, hCG-secreting and invasive. (Book p272)

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes the developmental origin and characteristics of the fetal chorion?
opts: Formed by chorion laeve on day 8; forms the outermost fetal membrane
Formed by ectoderm on day 10; forms the innermost membrane
An avascular membrane that contains no collagen
Formed from the secondary yolk sac on day 14
questions.exp: Chorion is formed by chorion laeve (cytotrophoblast) on Day 8 and is the outermost fetal membrane. (Book p272)

questions.q: The fetal amnion is derived embryologically from ectoderm on day 10 and is histologically notable for being:
opts: Avascular, without nerves or lymphatics, providing tensile strength
Highly vascularized with maternal capillary loops
Derived from endoderm and producing hCG
Richly innervated by fetal autonomic nerve fibers
questions.exp: Amnion is the innermost membrane formed from ectoderm on Day 10; it is avascular, aneural, lacks lymphatics, and gives tensile strength. (Book p272)

questions.q: In early embryonic development, the primary physiological functions of the yolk sac include:
opts: First site of fetal hematopoiesis and primary source of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
Synthesis of human placental lactogen and progesterone
Differentiation into the permanent umbilical arteries
Storage of maternal glycogen for the fetus
questions.exp: The yolk sac is the first site for fetal hematopoiesis and the primary early source of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). (Book p272)

questions.q: All of the following are derived from the inner cell mass EXCEPT:
questions.exp: The trophoblast (and hence syncytiotrophoblast) comes from the outer cell mass; the embryo, amnion and yolk sac come from the inner cell mass. (Book p272)

questions.q: Embryologically, the allantois is an endodermal diverticulum that connects the fetal hindgut to the:
questions.exp: The allantois is a diverticulum connecting the embryonic hindgut to the connecting stalk. (Book p273)

questions.q: During a lower-segment Cesarean section, what is the correct anatomical sequence of layers traversed from outside to inside to reach amniotic fluid?
opts: Skin → Abdominal wall muscles → Uterine serosa → Myometrium → Endometrium (Decidua) → Chorion → Amnion
Skin → Peritoneum → Amnion → Chorion → Myometrium → Decidua
Skin → Myometrium → Uterine serosa → Chorion → Decidua → Amnion
Skin → Abdominal wall → Decidua → Chorion → Uterine serosa → Myometrium → Amnion
questions.exp: Layers traversed: Skin, abdominal muscles, uterine serosa, myometrium, endometrium (decidua vera), chorion, and amnion. (Book p273)

questions.q: Rupture of the fetal membranes during active labor accelerates uterine contractions primarily through the local release of:
questions.exp: Membrane rupture releases PGF2α, which stimulates myometrial contractility and accelerates labor. (Book p273)

questions.q: Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT) is exclusively performed in assisted reproductive technology (ART) with the primary goal of:
opts: Selecting and transferring only genetically healthy embryos into the uterus
Inducing artificial zona hatching before cleavage
Preventing ectopic implantation in the fallopian tube
questions.exp: PGT involves genetic testing before implantation so that only healthy unaffected embryos are transferred into the uterus. (Book p273)

questions.q: Which of the following conditions represents a classic monogenic disorder frequently evaluated using PGT-M?
opts: Sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia
Down syndrome and Edwards syndrome exclusively
Congenital rubella syndrome and CMV infection
questions.exp: Monogenic disorders tested by PGT-M include sickle cell anemia, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia. (Book p273)

questions.q: In addition to single-gene monogenic mutations, PGT is indicated for detecting aneuploidies, HLA typing, and:
opts: Fetal hemoglobin variants in maternal blood
Neural tube defects via alpha-fetoprotein assay
questions.exp: PGT can detect aneuploidies, structural chromosomal rearrangements like balanced translocations, and enable HLA typing. (Book p273)

questions.q: A major developmental limitation of polar body biopsy during preimplantation genetic testing is that:
opts: Only maternally inherited genetic disorders can be tested
It causes inevitable destruction of the embryoblast
It cannot be performed in assisted reproduction
It transmits mitochondrial mutations to the fetus
questions.exp: The key drawback of polar body testing is that only maternally inherited genetic disorders can be evaluated. (Book p273)

questions.q: What is considered the safest and most reliable biopsy specimen for comprehensive PGT in modern ART?
opts: Trophectoderm biopsy at the blastocyst stage
questions.exp: Trophectoderm biopsy (sampling extraembryonic cells from the blastocyst) is the best material and avoids harming the inner cell mass. (Book p273)

questions.q: Fill up: Preimplantation genetic testing is performed on a biopsy of the ______ taken on day ______ of development.
questions.exp: Blastocyst-stage trophectoderm biopsy on day 5-6 is standard, because sampling the inner cell mass would risk the embryo itself. (Book p273)

questions.q: When calculating developmental milestones from the day of fertilization, the embryonic period spans:
opts: 3 to 8 weeks after fertilization (5th to 10th menstrual week)
questions.exp: The embryonic period spans 3–8 weeks after fertilization (5th to 10th week of pregnancy calculated from LMP). (Book p274)

questions.q: Teratogenic insult occurring during the first 2 weeks after fertilization (period of fertilized ovum) obeys the 'All-or-none law', meaning the conceptus:
opts: Either escapes injury completely or undergoes spontaneous abortion
Always develops major neural tube defects
questions.exp: During the first 2 weeks, exposure follows the all-or-none law: the embryo either completely recovers or aborts. (Book p274)

questions.q: The developmental window of maximum susceptibility to gross structural teratogenic malformations is the:
questions.exp: The embryonic period (3–8 weeks post-fertilization) is the period of active organogenesis and the most teratogenic period. (Book p274)

questions.q: What is the recognized maximum permissible cumulative radiation exposure dose throughout pregnancy?
questions.exp: The maximum permissible radiation exposure in pregnancy is 5 Rads (0.05 Gy). (Book p274)

questions.q: In utero radiation exposure exceeding 5 Rads increases the risk of intellectual disability, IUGR, and microcephaly, whereas a dose ≥10 Rads (≥0.1 Gy) causes:
questions.exp: Radiation exposure ≥10 Rads (≥0.1 Gy) causes severe fetal death, abortion, and gross structural devastation. (Book p274)

questions.q: A pregnant woman who underwent two accidental diagnostic abdominal X-rays before realizing she was pregnant (<0.5 Rads total) should be counseled to:
opts: Continue the pregnancy, as diagnostic X-rays fall well below 5 Rads
Undergo immediate medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)
questions.exp: Up to 2 diagnostic X-rays impart <0.5 Rads (far below the 5 Rad threshold); the pregnancy should be safely continued. (Book p274)

questions.q: Which of the following diagnostic imaging or contrast agents is absolutely contraindicated during pregnancy?
opts: Dental X-rays with lead abdominal shielding
questions.exp: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI, radioactive iodine, and paramagnetic contrast agents are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. (Book p274)

questions.q: A woman at 8 weeks of gestation has an abdominal CT scan; the calculated fetal dose is 4 rad (40 mGy). She asks whether the pregnancy must be terminated. What is the most appropriate counselling?
opts: Termination is not indicated — doses below 5 rad show no measurable rise in malformation or loss
Termination is advised — any exposure above 1 rad after 6 weeks causes microcephaly
Termination is advised — 4 rad lies above the 2 rad threshold for organogenic damage
Termination is not indicated — before 10 weeks radiation can only cause growth restriction
questions.exp: Below 5 rad there is no detectable increase in malformation, growth restriction or loss, so termination is not medically indicated. (Book p274)

questions.q: Which of the following medications is classified as an FDA Category X teratogen that is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.exp: Category X drugs are absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and include warfarin, thalidomide, isotretinoin, and DES. (Book p275)

questions.q: First-trimester gestational exposure to sodium valproate is classically associated with an increased incidence of:
opts: Neural tube defects (spina bifida) and cleft lip/palate
Epstein anomaly and floppy infant syndrome
questions.exp: Valproate exposure produces neural tube defects (NTDs), CNS defects, cardiac anomalies, and cleft lip/palate. (Book p275)

questions.q: The classic facial dysmorphology of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome (FAS) characteristically includes:
opts: Smooth/flat philtrum, thin vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures
Broad prominent philtrum, thick lips, and hypertelorism
Microtia, low-set ears, and cleft palate exclusively
Cloverleaf skull deformity and severe proptosis
questions.exp: FAS features growth restriction, microcephaly, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion border, and short palpebral fissures. (Book p275)

questions.q: Fetal hydantoin syndrome resulting from antenatal phenytoin exposure is characterized by midfacial hypoplasia, upturned nose, and:
opts: Distal digital and nail hypoplasia ± cardiac defects
Cranial nerve VI and VII palsies
questions.exp: Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome: midfacial hypoplasia, upturned nose, and distal digital/nail hypoplasia. (Book p275)

questions.q: Administration of ACE inhibitors or ARBs during the second and third trimesters produces fetal renal dysgenesis leading to:
opts: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
questions.exp: ACE inhibitors impair fetal renal perfusion, causing anuria, severe oligohydramnios, and hypoplastic lung development. (Book p275)

questions.q: In utero lithium exposure during cardiac organogenesis is classically associated with which congenital cardiac defect?
opts: Ebstein anomaly, with downward displacement of the tricuspid leaflets
Tetralogy of Fallot, with an overriding aorta and pulmonary stenosis
Coarctation of the aorta, with hypertension confined to the upper limbs
Patent ductus arteriosus, with a continuous machinery murmur
questions.exp: Lithium in cardiac organogenesis is classically linked to Ebstein anomaly, where the tricuspid leaflets are displaced into the right ventricle. (Book p275)

questions.sec: Teratogenic drugs: category X & specific malformations
questions.q: Match the drug with its classic fetal effect — 1) Warfarin 2) Sodium valproate 3) Lithium … A) Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve B) Nasal hypoplasia with stippled epiphyses C) Lumbosacral neural tube defect
questions.exp: Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and chondrodysplasia punctata, valproate causes neural tube defects, and lithium causes Ebstein anomaly. (Book p275)

questions.q: First-trimester exposure to the retinoid isotretinoin (used for cystic acne) characteristically causes:
opts: Microtia/anotia, CNS malformations, and cleft palate
Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the cervix
questions.exp: Isotretinoin causes craniofacial defects (microtia/anotia), CNS anomalies, thymic defects, and cleft palate. (Book p276)

questions.q: Thalidomide is notorious for causing which severe proximal limb reduction defect where hands or feet attach directly to the torso?
questions.exp: Thalidomide causes phocomelia (seal-like limbs due to severe proximal long-bone reduction) and stillbirth. (Book p276)

questions.q: Fetal Warfarin Syndrome (DiSaia syndrome) resulting from first-trimester exposure manifests as depressed nasal bridge, cataracts, and:
opts: Chondrodysplasia punctata with stippled epiphyses on radiography
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
questions.exp: Warfarin embryopathy causes defective cartilage formation (chondrodysplasia), stippled epiphyses, and nasal hypoplasia. (Book p276)

questions.q: Antenatal exposure to methotrexate during cranial bone ossification can cause severe craniosynostosis giving rise to a:
questions.exp: Methotrexate produces severe craniosynostosis leading to the classic cloverleaf skull deformity. (Book p276)

questions.q: Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) with DES-like teratogenicity, requires what minimum washout period before conception?
questions.exp: The minimum time gap between stopping tamoxifen and attempting pregnancy is 3 months. (Book p276)

questions.q: Failed first-trimester termination with misoprostol causes vascular disruption leading to limb defects and Moebius syndrome, which involves:
opts: Congenital 6th and 7th cranial nerve palsies with facial diplegia
Bilateral renal agenesis with flat facies
questions.exp: Misoprostol vascular disruption causes Moebius syndrome (6th and 7th cranial nerve palsy) and transverse limb reduction defects. (Book p276)

questions.q: Indomethacin is an effective tocolytic before 32 weeks, but administration beyond 32 weeks gestation is contraindicated because it causes:
opts: Premature in utero closure of the ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios
questions.exp: Beyond 32 weeks, indomethacin causes premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios. (Book p276)

questions.q: The most common congenital viral infection in humans and the leading non-genetic cause of congenital sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is:
questions.exp: CMV is both the most common congenital infection and the leading congenital cause of sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p277)

questions.q: What is the hallmark cranial sonographic or CT neuroimaging finding characteristic of Congenital Cytomegalovirus Syndrome?
questions.exp: Congenital CMV syndrome classically manifests with periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, chorioretinitis, and SNHL. (Book p277)

questions.q: The classic congenital triad of Toxoplasmosis consists of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and:
questions.exp: Congenital toxoplasmosis presents with hydrocephalus, diffuse intracranial calcifications, and chorioretinitis. (Book p277)

questions.q: What is the drug of choice for a pregnant woman diagnosed with acute toxoplasmosis, and what is given if fetal infection is confirmed?
opts: Spiramycin for mother; Pyrimethamine + Sulphadoxine for confirmed fetal infection
Pyrimethamine alone for mother; Acyclovir for fetus
Penicillin G for mother; Erythromycin for fetus
Ganciclovir for mother; Valganciclovir for fetus
questions.exp: Maternal toxoplasmosis is treated with spiramycin; if fetal infection is confirmed on amniocentesis, give pyrimethamine + sulphadoxine. (Book p277)

questions.q: The classical Gregg's triad of Congenital Rubella Syndrome following first-trimester maternal viremia comprises:
opts: Cataracts/glaucoma, cardiac defects (PDA/pulmonary stenosis), and SNHL
Spina bifida, clubfoot, and renal dysgenesis
questions.exp: Congenital rubella syndrome causes heart disease (PDA/pulmonary stenosis), eye anomalies (cataract/glaucoma), and sensorineural hearing loss. (Book p277)

questions.q: A pregnant woman in the first trimester is found to be rubella-IgG negative on antenatal screening. The recommended management is to:
opts: Administer the MMR vaccine after delivery and advise avoiding pregnancy for 1 month post-vaccine
Administer MMR vaccine immediately in the first trimester
Give high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) within 24 hours
questions.exp: Rubella vaccine is a live vaccine contraindicated in pregnancy; vaccinate postpartum and advise avoiding pregnancy for 1 month. (Book p277)

questions.q: All of the following are recognised features of congenital cytomegalovirus infection EXCEPT:
questions.exp: PDA and pulmonary stenosis belong to congenital rubella; CMV gives periventricular calcification, chorioretinitis and sensorineural deafness. (Book p277)

questions.q: Congenital varicella syndrome resulting from early maternal chickenpox exposure classically presents with:
opts: Cicatricial zigzag skin scars in a dermatomal pattern and limb hypoplasia
Severe neonatal jaundice and bilateral cataracts
Patent ductus arteriosus and congenital glaucoma
questions.exp: Congenital varicella syndrome is characterized by cicatricial skin scarring along dermatomes and hypoplastic limb deformities. (Book p278)

questions.q: The highest risk of severe, life-threatening neonatal varicella occurs when maternal chickenpox rash erupts within:
opts: 5 days before to 2 days after delivery
questions.exp: Maternal chickenpox from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery exposes the neonate to severe varicella without maternal antibodies. (Book p278)

questions.q: Maternal Parvovirus B19 infection in pregnancy targets fetal erythroid progenitor cells, leading to profound fetal anemia, high-output failure, and:
opts: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
questions.exp: Parvovirus B19 lyses erythroid progenitors, causing fetal anemia, high-output heart failure, hydrops fetalis, and polyhydramnios. (Book p278)

questions.q: Which non-invasive Doppler ultrasound parameter is the investigation of choice to assess the severity of fetal anemia in Parvovirus B19 infection?
opts: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) peak systolic velocity
questions.exp: Middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler peak systolic velocity is the investigation of choice to detect and monitor fetal anemia. (Book p278)

questions.q: Zika virus exhibits strong placental tropism via TIM-1 and TAM-AXL receptors on Hofbauer cells, causing fetal brain devastation characterized by:
opts: Severe cortical brain atrophy, microcephaly, and arthrogryposis/limb contractures
questions.exp: Zika virus attacks placental Hofbauer cells and fetal neural tissue, causing severe cortical atrophy, microcephaly, and arthrogryposis. (Book p278)

questions.q: In a pregnant woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), transplacental transfer of which maternal autoantibodies causes congenital complete heart block in the fetus?
questions.exp: Anti-Ro and Anti-La antibodies cross the placenta to cause inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node, producing complete heart block. (Book p278)

questions.q: The human placenta is morphologically and histologically classified as:
questions.exp: Human placenta is discoid in shape, deciduate (sheds after birth), and hemochorial (villi bathe directly in maternal blood). (Book p279)

questions.q: At term, what is the average weight of the human placenta and the typical placenta-to-fetal weight ratio?
questions.exp: The term placenta weighs ~500 grams, with a placenta-to-fetal weight ratio of 1:6. (Book p279)

questions.q: At what gestational age is the weight of the developing human placenta equal to the weight of the fetus?
questions.exp: At 17 weeks of gestation, the weight of the placenta equals the weight of the fetus. (Book p279)

questions.q: Under normal term physiological conditions, the diameter and central thickness of the placenta measure approximately:
opts: Diameter: 15–20 cm; Thickness at center: 2.5–4 cm
Diameter: 25–30 cm; Thickness at center: 5–6 cm
Diameter: 8–10 cm; Thickness at center: 1–2 cm
Diameter: 10–12 cm; Thickness at center: 0.5–1 cm
questions.exp: The normal placenta measures 15–20 cm in diameter and 2.5–4 cm in central thickness. (Book p279)

questions.q: Placentomegaly is defined as a placental thickness exceeding 4 cm, which can be caused by:
opts: Maternal diabetes, hydrops fetalis, and congenital syphilis
Preeclampsia and severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
Post-term dysmaturity syndrome and severe oligohydramnios
questions.exp: Placentomegaly (>4 cm thick) is caused by diabetes, multifetal gestation, hydrops fetalis, severe fetal anemia, and syphilis. (Book p279)

questions.q: Which of the following clinical conditions characteristically results in an abnormally small, thin, hypoplastic placenta?
questions.exp: Uteroplacental insufficiency, pre-eclampsia (PIH), and IUGR characteristically result in a small, underperfused placenta. (Book p279)

questions.q: Fill up: At term the placenta weighs about ______ g, which is roughly ______ of the fetal weight.
questions.exp: The term placenta weighs about 500 g and its ratio to the fetus is about 1:6. (Book p279)

questions.q: Which set of features accurately describes the fetal surface compared to the maternal surface of the human placenta?
opts: Fetal: shiny, grey-blue, forms 4/5th; Maternal: dull, fleshy-red, forms 1/5th with 15–20 cotyledons
Fetal: dull red with cotyledons, forms 1/5th; Maternal: covered by amnion, forms 4/5th
Fetal: derived from decidua basalis; Maternal: derived from chorion frondosum
Fetal: divided by decidual septa into 30 lobes; Maternal: smooth and completely avascular
questions.exp: The fetal surface forms 4/5th (shiny, covered by amnion/chorion frondosum); the maternal surface forms 1/5th (dull red decidua basalis, 15–20 cotyledons). (Book p280)

questions.q: What is the correct anatomical sequence of histological layers composing the placental membrane/barrier from maternal blood to fetal blood?
opts: Syncytiotrophoblast → Cytotrophoblast → Extraembryonic mesoderm → Fetal capillary endothelium
Cytotrophoblast → Syncytiotrophoblast → Amniotic epithelium → Capillary wall
Syncytiotrophoblast → Decidua basalis → Mesoderm → Fetal blood
questions.exp: Placental barrier from outside to inside: Syncytiotrophoblast, Cytotrophoblast, Extraembryonic mesoderm, and Fetal capillary endothelium. (Book p281)

questions.q: Primary chorionic villi appear on day 13 after fertilization and are histologically composed of:
opts: A cytotrophoblastic core surrounded by syncytiotrophoblast (trophoblastic shell)
Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, and a mesodermal core
Trophoblastic shell, mesenchyme, and functional fetal capillaries
Amniotic ectoderm and maternal vascular lacunae
questions.exp: Primary villi (Day 13) consist of a central cytotrophoblast core covered by syncytiotrophoblast (trophoblastic shell). (Book p281)

questions.q: Secondary chorionic villi form on day 16 after fertilization when which structure invades the core of the primary villus?
questions.exp: Secondary villi form on Day 16 when extraembryonic mesoderm grows into the center of the trophoblastic shell. (Book p281)

questions.q: Tertiary chorionic villi are definitively established on day 17 after fertilization by the appearance of:
opts: Fetal blood vessels / capillaries within the mesodermal core
questions.exp: Tertiary villi are established on Day 17 when fetal blood vessels and capillaries differentiate within the villous core. (Book p281)

questions.q: The total blood volume contained within the human term placenta is 500 ml, which is partitioned into:
opts: 350 ml of fetal blood (in villi) and 150 ml of maternal blood (in intervillous space)
250 ml of fetal blood and 250 ml of maternal blood
150 ml of fetal blood and 350 ml of maternal blood
450 ml of fetal blood and 50 ml of maternal blood
questions.exp: Placental blood totals 500 ml: 350 ml fetal blood within villous capillaries and 150 ml maternal blood in the intervillous space. (Book p281)

questions.q: During physiological trophoblastic invasion, cytotrophoblast cells remodel maternal spiral arteries by replacing their muscular coats, which converts them into:
opts: Dilated, flaccid, low-resistance vessels that deliver high blood flow to the intervillous space
Narrow, highly coiled, high-resistance muscular sphincters
Venous sinusoids that drain retroplacental clots
questions.exp: Cytotrophoblasts replace the muscular media of spiral arteries, transforming them into dilated low-resistance conduits that maximize IVS flow. (Book p281)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries is TRUE?
opts: Extravillous trophoblast replaces the musculoelastic media of spiral arteries by 20-24 weeks
Endovascular trophoblast invasion stops at the decidua and never reaches the myometrial segment
Spiral arteries keep their smooth muscle throughout pregnancy, so intervillous flow stays pulsatile
Cytotrophoblast plugs persist until the third trimester and only dissolve after 28 weeks
questions.exp: The second wave of trophoblast invasion converts spiral arteries into low-resistance flaccid tubes by 20-24 weeks; plugs disappear by 10-12 weeks. (Book p281)

questions.q: In the developing human placenta, uteroplacental and fetoplacental circulations are established on which post-fertilization days?
opts: Uteroplacental by Day 12–13; Fetoplacental by Day 17
Uteroplacental by Day 6; Fetoplacental by Day 14
Uteroplacental by Day 28; Fetoplacental by Day 32
Uteroplacental by Day 20; Fetoplacental by Day 24
questions.exp: Uteroplacental circulation in the IVS is established by Day 12–13; fetoplacental circulation in the villi is established by Day 17. (Book p282)

questions.q: In fetoplacental circulation, physiological gas and nutrient transport between placenta and fetus is conducted by:
opts: Umbilical vein carrying oxygenated blood to fetus; two umbilical arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to placenta
Two umbilical veins carrying oxygenated blood; one umbilical artery carrying deoxygenated blood
Umbilical artery carrying oxygenated blood; umbilical vein carrying waste to placenta
Spiral arteries carrying fetal blood; uterine veins carrying maternal blood
questions.exp: The single umbilical vein transports oxygenated blood from placenta to fetus; two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood. (Book p282)

questions.q: At term gestation, what are the normal volumetric blood flow rates through the uteroplacental space and the total uterine circulation?
questions.exp: At term, uteroplacental blood flow is 500–700 ml/min, total uterine blood flow is 750 ml/min, and fetoplacental flow is 400 ml/min. (Book p282)

questions.q: A placental cotyledon, the basic functional unit of the human placenta, is anatomically defined as the territory supplied by:
opts: One main stem villus and its branching hierarchy
The entire chorion laeve combined with amnion
Two adjacent decidual septa without villous tissue
questions.exp: A placental cotyledon is the functional unit of the placenta supplied by one main stem villus and all its branches. (Book p282)

questions.q: Nitabuch's layer is a zone of fibrinoid degeneration situated between the invading trophoblast and decidua basalis whose primary role is to:
opts: Limit the invasive penetration of the blastocyst into the myometrium
Prevent maternal immunological rejection of syncytiotrophoblast
Stimulate continuous production of human placental lactogen
Facilitate immediate postpartum separation of the amnion
questions.exp: Nitabuch's layer is a zone of fibrinoid degeneration between blastocyst and decidua basalis that limits deep invasion into the myometrium. (Book p282)

questions.q: Congenital or iatrogenic absence of Nitabuch's layer permits blastocyst invasion directly into the myometrium, producing:
questions.exp: Absence of Nitabuch's layer allows chorionic villi to attach directly to myometrium, causing placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). (Book p282)

questions.q: Fill up: The term placenta contains about ______ cotyledons, and each is supplied by a single ______ artery.
questions.exp: There are roughly 15-20 cotyledons, each supplied by one truncal (stem villous) artery arising from the chorionic plate vessels. (Book p282)

questions.q: In addition to acting as an endocrine organ, the placenta carries out crucial fetal life-support functions, the most vital of which is:
opts: Immunological suppression of all maternal IgG
Thermal regulation through brown fat synthesis
Direct erythropoiesis for the fetal marrow
questions.exp: The two primary placental functions are respiratory gas exchange and hormone production. (Book p283)

questions.q: The oxygen saturation and partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) in maternal intervillous space blood normally equal those in the umbilical vein, measuring:
questions.exp: Oxygen saturation in the IVS and umbilical vein is 65–75%, with a partial pressure of O2 around 30–35 mm Hg. (Book p283)

questions.q: In a non-conception menstrual cycle, the corpus luteum reaches its maximum morphological size and peak progesterone secretion on:
opts: Day 22 of the cycle (8 days after ovulation)
Day 14 of the cycle (day of ovulation)
Day 1 of the cycle (onset of menses)
questions.exp: The corpus luteum attains maximum size and peak progesterone production on Day 22 of the cycle (8 days post-ovulation). (Book p283)

questions.q: When fertilization occurs, luteolysis of the corpus luteum is prevented by which hormone secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast from day 8 post-fertilization?
questions.exp: Syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG from Day 8 after fertilization (Day 22 of cycle), which rescues the corpus luteum from degeneration. (Book p283)

questions.q: A 29-year-old at 6 weeks of gestation has a corpus luteum removed at laparotomy for a large haemorrhagic cyst. If no hormonal support is given, what is the most likely outcome?
opts: Pregnancy loss, because the luteo-placental shift is not complete until 8-10 weeks
Normal continuation, because hCG alone maintains the decidua from the fourth week onward
Normal continuation, because the fetal adrenal axis takes over progesterone synthesis immediately
Preterm labour at 32 weeks, since progesterone is what suppresses myometrial contractility
questions.exp: Before the luteo-placental shift at 8-10 weeks the corpus luteum is the sole source of progesterone, so its removal without support causes loss. (Book p283)

questions.q: The functional lifespan of the corpus luteum of pregnancy, maintaining early gestational hormone support, is approximately:
questions.exp: The lifespan of the corpus luteum of pregnancy is 10–12 weeks. (Book p284)

questions.q: The critical transition known as the luteal-placental shift, during which the placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum, occurs at:
questions.exp: Progesterone originates from the CL until 7 weeks, shifts between 8–10 weeks, and is solely produced by the placenta after 10 weeks. (Book p284)

questions.q: An asymptomatic simple ovarian cyst detected on first-trimester ultrasound should be managed conservatively without surgery because surgical excision before 7 weeks will cause:
opts: Immediate miscarriage due to loss of luteal progesterone support
questions.exp: The cyst is almost certainly the corpus luteum; removal before 7 weeks removes essential progesterone and precipitates abortion. (Book p284)

questions.q: The human placenta is incapable of de novo cholesterol synthesis from acetate; it synthesizes progesterone using which circulating maternal precursor?
questions.exp: Placental progesterone is synthesized directly from circulating maternal cholesterol. (Book p284)

questions.q: The essential physiological action of progesterone in sustaining pregnancy throughout gestation is to:
opts: Maintain profound myometrial smooth muscle relaxation and prevent preterm labor
Stimulate active myometrial oxytocin receptor expression
Promote rapid cervical ripening and effacement
Increase peripheral vascular resistance to maintain blood pressure
questions.exp: Progesterone acts as a uterine smooth muscle relaxant that maintains quiescence and prevents preterm labor. (Book p284)

questions.q: Because the human placenta lacks 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-desmolase, it relies on which fetal adrenal precursor for estrogen biosynthesis?
questions.exp: The placenta requires fetal adrenal DHEA-S because it lacks the 17α-hydroxylase and desmolase needed to convert C21 steroids to C19 androgens. (Book p284)

questions.q: Which two placental enzymes convert fetal adrenal DHEA-sulfate into active estrogens (estrone and estradiol)?
questions.exp: Placental sulfatase removes the sulfate from DHEA-S, and aromatase converts the androgens into estrogens. (Book p284)

questions.q: Match the following about placental steroidogenesis — 1) Substrate the placenta takes from the mother 2) Enzyme pair the placenta lacks 3) Principal estrogen of pregnancy … A) 17-alpha-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase B) Maternal LDL cholesterol C) Estriol
questions.exp: The placenta uses maternal LDL cholesterol, lacks 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, and makes estriol from fetal DHEA-S and 16-alpha-OH-DHEA-S. (Book p284)

questions.q: The physiological endocrine trigger initiating the onset of spontaneous labor contractions at term involves:
opts: Functional withdrawal of progesterone accompanied by an increase in estrogen
Sudden surge in maternal progesterone and decrease in estrogen
Complete cessation of placental relaxin and hPL
Acute drop in fetal cortisol and oxytocin
questions.exp: Onset of labor is triggered by functional progesterone withdrawal combined with elevated estrogen, initiating uterine contractions. (Book p285)

questions.q: Fetal anencephaly is classically complicated by post-term pregnancy because the absence of the hypothalamus and pituitary results in:
opts: Adrenal hypoplasia with absence of DHEA-S, leading to deficient placental estrogen production
Excessive secretion of human placental lactogen
questions.exp: In anencephaly, adrenal hypoplasia means no DHEA-S is produced; lack of placental estrogen fails to trigger labor, causing post-term pregnancy. (Book p285)

questions.q: In addition to fetal anencephaly and wrong menstrual dates (most common), endocrine causes of post-term pregnancy include:
opts: Placental sulfatase and placental aromatase deficiencies
Elevated hCG levels and hyperemesis gravidarum
questions.exp: Placental sulfatase deficiency, aromatase deficiency, and intrauterine fetal death cause deficient estrogen and post-term gestation. (Book p285)

questions.q: Placental and luteal relaxin mediates which physiological cardiovascular and musculoskeletal adaptations during pregnancy?
opts: Joint laxity (pelvic ligaments), smooth muscle relaxation, decreased PVR, and increased GFR
Closure of the ductus arteriosus and decreased renal blood flow
Elevation of systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure
questions.exp: Relaxin causes pelvic joint laxity, uterine quiescence, systemic vasodilation (decreased PVR), and increased renal blood flow/GFR. (Book p285)

questions.q: Human placental lactogen (hPL), synthesized by the syncytiotrophoblast, exhibits 96% structural homology with which pituitary hormone?
questions.exp: hPL is a polypeptide hormone synthesized by syncytiotrophoblasts that has 96% structural homology with growth hormone. (Book p285)

questions.q: What is the biological half-life (T1/2) of human placental lactogen in maternal plasma?
questions.exp: The biological half-life of hPL is 15 minutes (in contrast to hCG which is 36 hours). (Book p285)

questions.q: Production of hPL begins at the 3rd week, peaks at 36 weeks, and serves as an indicator of placental mass whose primary metabolic action is to:
opts: Exert an anti-insulin diabetogenic effect, sparing maternal glucose and amino acids for the fetus
Inhibit maternal lipolysis and increase maternal glycogen storage
questions.exp: hPL produces maternal insulin resistance (diabetogenic effect) and lipolysis, ensuring continuous glucose availability for the fetus. (Book p286)

questions.q: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a heterodimeric glycoprotein whose α-subunit is structurally identical to that of LH, FSH, and TSH, while biological specificity is determined by its:
questions.exp: The alpha subunit is shared with LH, FSH, and TSH; the beta subunit is unique and imparts hormone-specific biological identity. (Book p286)

questions.q: In early embryonic development, the initial stimulus prompting fetal testicular Leydig cells to produce testosterone for male differentiation is:
questions.exp: Placental hCG provides the initial stimulus for fetal Leydig cells to synthesize and secrete testosterone. (Book p286)

questions.q: In normal gestation, beta-hCG can be detected earliest in maternal serum and maternal urine at:
opts: Serum: 8 days post-fertilization (Day 22); Urine: Day of missed period (Day 28)
Serum: Day of missed period; Urine: 8 weeks of gestation
Serum: 14 days post-fertilization; Urine: 3 weeks after missed period
Serum: 30 hours post-fertilization; Urine: Day 20 of cycle
questions.exp: hCG is detectable in blood as early as 8 days after fertilization (Day 22 of cycle) and in urine by the day of the missed period. (Book p286)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about human chorionic gonadotropin is TRUE?
opts: The beta subunit is hCG-specific and is what assays measure; the alpha subunit is shared with TSH, LH and FSH
Serum hCG keeps rising through the second trimester and peaks only at around 28 weeks
A doubling time slower than seven days is entirely normal between 4 and 8 weeks of gestation
hCG first appears in maternal blood only after implantation is complete at about day 14
questions.exp: hCG peaks at 8-10 weeks and then falls; the beta subunit is assay-specific, and hCG is detectable from about day 8-9, well before day 14. (Book p286)

questions.q: Serum levels of hCG peak at approximately 10 weeks of gestation (60–80 days) reaching what typical concentration?
questions.exp: hCG peaks at 10 weeks (60–80 days) at ~100,000 IU/L (10^5), declining to a plateau of ~10,000 IU/L by 16 weeks. (Book p287)

questions.q: What is the biological plasma half-life of hCG, and how soon after delivery does it become undetectable in maternal serum?
opts: Half-life: 36 hours; undetectable by 2 weeks postpartum
Half-life: 15 minutes; undetectable by 24 hours postpartum
Half-life: 7 days; undetectable by 6 months postpartum
Half-life: 12 hours; undetectable by 6 weeks postpartum
questions.exp: The plasma half-life of hCG is 36 hours; levels clear to zero by 2 weeks after normal delivery (2–4 weeks post-abortion). (Book p287)

questions.q: In a patient presenting at ≤4 weeks gestation with an empty uterus on ultrasound, a 48-hour repeat beta-hCG that rises by only 15% most strongly suggests:
opts: A completely normal viable intrauterine pregnancy
questions.exp: A viable intrauterine pregnancy rises by 33%–66% in 48 hours; a suboptimal rise <30–33% strongly suggests an ectopic pregnancy. (Book p287)

questions.q: The discriminatory zone—the serum beta-hCG titer at which an intrauterine gestational sac must be visualized—is defined as:
questions.exp: An intrauterine sac must be seen at beta-hCG ≥2000 IU/L on TVS and ≥6500 IU/L on TAS; absence indicates an ectopic pregnancy. (Book p288)

questions.q: Which of the following clinical conditions is characteristically associated with pathologically elevated serum beta-hCG levels?
opts: Molar pregnancy, multifetal gestation, and Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
Intrauterine growth restriction and placental sulfatase deficiency
questions.exp: hCG is elevated in twin pregnancies, molar pregnancy/GTN, Rh-negative hydrops, and Down syndrome (Trisomy 21). (Book p288)

questions.q: Anatomically, placenta previa is defined as abnormal implantation of the placenta within the:
questions.exp: Placenta previa is located in the lower uterine segment, rather than the normal upper uterine segment. (Book p289)

questions.q: In the Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS), when chorionic villi invade deeply into the myometrial muscular wall without reaching serosa, it is designated as:
questions.exp: Accreta attaches to superficial myometrium; increta invades deeply into myometrium; percreta penetrates through to serosa or bladder. (Book p289)

questions.q: Placenta percreta represents the most aggressive form of morbidly adherent placenta, wherein chorionic villi:
opts: Penetrate through the entire myometrium to the uterine serosa or adjacent pelvic organs
Attach superficially to the basal layer of the endometrium
Are confined strictly to the decidua basalis without muscular contact
Are attached to an accessory placental lobe across membranes
questions.exp: In placenta percreta, chorionic villi penetrate through the entire myometrium and uterine serosa, potentially invading the urinary bladder. (Book p289)

questions.q: Placenta bilobata (bipartita) is morphologically characterized by:
opts: Placenta divided into two roughly equal lobes connected by blood vessels with a single umbilical cord
Two separate placentas with two separate umbilical cords
One major placenta with a tiny rudimentary accessory lobe
A central depression encircled by a double fold of membranes
questions.exp: Placenta bilobata consists of two roughly equal lobes connected by vessels, with a single umbilical cord (unlike twin placentas). (Book p289)

questions.q: Placenta succenturiata features a separate accessory lobe connected by intramembranous vessels, presenting clinical risks of:
opts: Retention of the succenturiate lobe causing PPH and placenta previa
Immediate fetal phocomelia with amputation of the digits
Complete congenital heart block appearing in the newborn
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus in the fetus
questions.exp: Placenta succenturiata has a separate accessory lobe joined by intramembranous vessels, risking a retained succenturiate lobe with postpartum hemorrhage and an increased risk of placenta previa. (Book p289)

questions.q: All of the following predispose to placenta accreta spectrum EXCEPT:
opts: Grand multiparity without any uterine surgery
Previous caesarean section with an anterior low-lying placenta
Previous endometrial curettage or Asherman syndrome
questions.exp: Accreta spectrum needs a deficient decidua from endometrial damage — scar, curettage, previa or myomectomy; parity alone does not scar the myometrium. (Book p289)

questions.q: In an extrachorial placenta, the maternal surface is larger than the fetal surface, resulting in:
opts: Fetal membranes failing to extend to the placental margin, forming a ring on the fetal surface
The umbilical cord inserting directly into the cervical canal
The chorionic villi attaching directly to the ovarian surface
questions.exp: In extrachorial placenta, maternal surface exceeds the fetal surface, so membranes insert inward and form a ring around the fetal surface. (Book p290)

questions.q: A circumvallate placenta is distinguished on gross examination by a thick, raised, rolled white ring at the margin with a central depression, predisposing to:
opts: Intrauterine growth restriction and antepartum hemorrhage from abruption
Fetal macrosomia together with polyhydramnios in the third trimester
Down syndrome and maternal hyperthyroidism in the index pregnancy
Post-term pregnancy with a persistently high serum hCG level
questions.exp: A circumvallate placenta shows a thick raised rolled white ring at the margin with central depression, and predisposes to IUGR and antepartum hemorrhage (abruptio placentae). (Book p290)

questions.q: Unlike circumvallate placenta, a circummarginate placenta exhibits a flat, smooth transition between membranes and placenta at the same level and is:
opts: Clinically benign and of no significant clinical consequence
An absolute indication for immediate Cesarean section
Associated with a 50% incidence of fetal mortality
questions.exp: Circummarginate placenta shows a flat, smooth transition without a raised fold and carries no clinical significance. (Book p290)

questions.q: A placenta in which the umbilical cord is inserted directly into the lateral placental margin rather than near the center is termed a:
questions.exp: In battledore placenta, the umbilical cord is attached to the lateral margin of the placenta like a table tennis bat. (Book p291)

questions.q: In velamentous cord insertion, the umbilical cord inserts into the fetal membranes away from the placenta, leaving fetal vessels vulnerable because:
opts: Protective Wharton's jelly is absent as vessels traverse the bare membranes
The umbilical vein is completely obliterated
The vessels are surrounded by a thick calcified sheath
The vessels carry only maternal blood
questions.exp: In velamentous insertion, cord vessels run through membranes devoid of protective Wharton's jelly, predisposing them to tearing. (Book p291)

questions.q: The catastrophic consequence of vasa previa occurs when membrane rupture tears unsupported fetal vessels crossing the internal os, producing:
opts: Rapid fetal exsanguination and high perinatal mortality
Severe maternal hemorrhagic shock with normal fetal heart
questions.exp: Vasa previa involves fetal vessels traversing the internal os; rupture causes direct fetal hemorrhage and catastrophic perinatal mortality. (Book p291)

questions.q: Type 1 vasa previa is caused by velamentous cord insertion, while Type 2 vasa previa results from:
opts: Vessels traversing between the lobes in placenta bilobata or succenturiata
Dehiscence of a previous caesarean section scar in the lower segment
Complete congenital absence of the single umbilical vein
A circumvallate ring forming around the margin of the placenta
questions.exp: Type 1 vasa previa comes from velamentous cord insertion, while type 2 results from vessels traversing between the lobes in placenta bilobata or placenta succenturiata. (Book p292)

questions.q: What is the investigation of choice (IOC) for vasa previa, and what is the definitive delivery recommendation upon antenatal diagnosis?
opts: Color Doppler ultrasound; Elective Cesarean section at 34–37 weeks
Digital vaginal examination; Induction of labor at 39 weeks
Non-stress test alone; Expectant management until spontaneous rupture
questions.exp: Color Doppler ultrasound is the IOC; antenatal detection mandates elective Cesarean delivery at 34–37 weeks (ARM is contraindicated). (Book p292)

questions.q: In a laboring patient presenting with painless vaginal bleeding immediately following amniotomy, which finding specifically points to vasa previa over placenta previa?
opts: Profound fetal distress (bradycardia/sinusoidal CTG) entirely out of proportion to slight maternal vaginal bleeding
Profuse maternal bleeding with completely normal fetal heart tones
The presence of a visible retroplacental clot on ultrasound
A high maternal pulse pressure with maternal hypovolemia
questions.exp: In vasa previa, the blood lost is fetal, causing severe, rapid fetal distress out of proportion to the minimal external blood seen. (Book p292)

questions.sec: Cord insertion anomalies, vasa previa & Apt test
questions.q: At 38 weeks, membranes rupture spontaneously and are immediately followed by fresh vaginal bleeding and fetal bradycardia. Vaginal blood is mixed with water; after adding alkali the supernatant stays pink. What is the diagnosis and the immediate step?
opts: Vasa previa with fetal haemorrhage — immediate caesarean section
Placental abruption with maternal bleeding — stabilise and aim for vaginal delivery
Bloody show from cervical dilatation — reassure and await spontaneous labour
Uterine rupture — laparotomy and repair of the uterine scar
questions.exp: A positive Apt test (alkali-resistant fetal haemoglobin turning the supernatant pink) means the blood is fetal — vasa previa demands immediate caesarean. (Book p292)

questions.q: The Apt test (Singer's alkali denaturation test) differentiates fetal from maternal vaginal bleeding by adding 1% NaOH or KOH to vaginal blood because:
opts: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is alkali-resistant (remains pink), while adult hemoglobin (HbA) denatures (turns yellow-brown)
Adult hemoglobin is alkali-resistant, while fetal hemoglobin rapidly precipitates
Maternal platelets clump immediately in the presence of alkali
Fetal leukocytes lyse and release peroxidase enzymes
questions.exp: HbF is alkali-resistant, so vaginal blood containing HbF remains pink (+ve Apt test = vasa previa); HbA denatures to brown (placenta previa). (Book p293)

questions.q: Which comparison correctly contrasts the Apt test with the Kleihauer-Betke test?
opts: Apt test: qualitative test for vasa previa using NaOH; Kleihauer-Betke: quantitative acid elution test to dose anti-D in Rh -ve mothers
Apt test: quantitative test for fetal anemia; Kleihauer-Betke: qualitative test for placenta accreta
Both tests utilize identical alkaline reagents on maternal urine
Kleihauer-Betke test is used exclusively to diagnose ectopic pregnancy
questions.exp: Apt test is a qualitative alkali test for vasa previa; Kleihauer-Betke is a quantitative acid elution test on maternal blood to calculate anti-D dose. (Book p293)

questions.q: What is the chronological sequence of anatomical sites of hematopoiesis and primary hemoglobin types during embryonic and fetal development?
opts: <6 weeks: Yolk sac (Gower/Portland); 6–30 weeks: Liver (HbF); ≥20 weeks: Bone marrow (HbA)
<6 weeks: Liver; 6–30 weeks: Spleen; ≥20 weeks: Yolk sac
<6 weeks: Bone marrow; 6–30 weeks: Yolk sac; ≥20 weeks: Liver
<6 weeks: Thymus; 6–30 weeks: Bone marrow; ≥20 weeks: Spleen
questions.exp: Hematopoiesis originates in yolk sac (<6 wks, embryonic Hb), shifts to liver (6–30 wks, HbF), and establishes in bone marrow (≥20 wks, HbA). (Book p293)

questions.q: Fill up: Fetal erythropoiesis begins in the ______, and the predominant haemoglobin at term is ______.
questions.exp: The mesoblastic (yolk-sac) phase starts first, and HbF still predominates at term, with HbA rising only after birth. (Book p293)

questions.q: At birth, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) comprises approximately 75%–90% of total hemoglobin, but by 6 months of age it normally declines to:
questions.exp: At birth, HbF accounts for 75%–90% of total hemoglobin, falling to approximately 1% by 6 months of postnatal life. (Book p294)

questions.q: What is the normal physiological hemoglobin concentration in a healthy term newborn infant?
questions.exp: The normal hemoglobin concentration in a healthy term neonate is 16–18 g/dL. (Book p294)

questions.q: During the third stage of labor, normal physiological placental detachment occurs along which histological cleavage plane?
opts: Zona spongiosa of the decidua basalis
Zona compacta of the decidua basalis
questions.exp: Normal placental separation occurs cleanly through the spongy layer (zona spongiosa) of the decidua basalis. (Book p294)

questions.q: Which features correctly distinguish the Schultze method from the Duncan method of placental separation?
opts: Schultze: central separation, shiny fetal surface first; Duncan: peripheral separation, dull maternal surface first
Schultze: peripheral separation, dull maternal surface first; Duncan: central separation, shiny fetal surface first
Schultze: continuous bleeding from the start; Duncan: bleeding appears only after expulsion
Schultze: peripheral detachment with no retroplacental clot; Duncan: central detachment with a large clot
questions.exp: Schultze (80%) separates centrally, the shiny fetal surface is expelled first and bleeding is seen only after expulsion; Duncan (20%) separates peripherally, the dull maternal surface is expelled first and bleeding is continuous. (Book p294)

questions.q: The four classic clinical signs confirming complete placental separation in the third stage of labor are:
opts: Gush of blood, umbilical/suprapubic bulge, fundus rising and becoming firm/globular, and permanent lengthening of the cord
Sudden maternal hypotension, severe fetal bradycardia, uterine relaxation, and cord shortening
Absence of vaginal bleeding, flattening of the fundus, disappearance of the cord, and pelvic pain
