Immediate cervical dilatation to 10 cm, descent of presenting part, caput formation, and crowning
questions.exp: The 4 signs of separation are: a sudden gush of blood, suprapubic bulge, uterine fundus rising and becoming globular, and permanent cord lengthening. (Book p294)

questions.q: What are the normal physical and biochemical properties of term amniotic fluid?
questions.exp: Normal amniotic fluid has a specific gravity of 1.008–1.010, slightly alkaline pH (7.2), and osmolarity of ~260 mOsm/L. (Book p295)

questions.q: The volume of amniotic fluid reaches its physiological maximum of approximately 1000 ml at 32–34 weeks, thereafter declining to:
opts: 800 ml at 40 weeks (term) and ~200 ml at 42 weeks (post-term)
500 ml at 36 weeks and 100 ml at term
1500 ml at 38 weeks and 1200 ml at term
800 ml at 36 weeks and remaining at 800 ml until 43 weeks
questions.exp: Amniotic volume peaks at 1 L at 32–34 weeks, drops to ~800 ml at term (40 weeks), and declines sharply to ~200 ml at 42 weeks. (Book p295)

questions.q: What is the primary physiological source of amniotic fluid production after 20 weeks of gestation?
opts: Maternal transudate across the vaginal mucosa
Direct amniotic epithelial active water secretion
questions.exp: After 20 weeks, fetal urine is the main contributor to amniotic fluid, producing ~1000 ml/day at term. (Book p295)

questions.q: Transudation of fluid across fetal skin ceases to contribute to amniotic fluid when cutaneous keratinization completes at:
questions.exp: Keratinization of fetal skin is complete by 22–25 weeks of pregnancy, after which transudation across the skin stops. (Book p295)

questions.q: The primary mechanism responsible for clearing and maintaining normal amniotic fluid turnover is:
opts: Fetal swallowing (500–1000 ml/day absorbed by the fetal gut)
Intramembranous transport into maternal pelvic veins
Direct filtration across the umbilical cord Wharton's jelly
Passive diffusion across maternal abdominal wall muscles
questions.exp: Fetal swallowing (500–1000 ml/day) is the primary clearance pathway; impaired swallowing results in polyhydramnios. (Book p295)

questions.q: Match the amniotic fluid colour with its usual meaning — 1) Golden yellow 2) Green 3) Port-wine or red-brown … A) Meconium staining B) Rh isoimmunisation with bilirubin C) Old blood, as in abruptio placentae
questions.exp: Golden fluid means bilirubin from haemolysis, green means meconium, and port-wine or red-brown means old intrauterine bleeding. (Book p295)

questions.q: On amniocentesis or artificial rupture of membranes, normal amniotic fluid appears:
opts: Straw-colored at term and completely colorless in preterm gestation
Golden-yellow at term and deep green preterm
Port-wine colored at term and cloudy white preterm
Dark brown at term and straw-colored preterm
questions.exp: Normal amniotic fluid is colorless and watery in early/preterm pregnancy, becoming pale straw-colored at term. (Book p296)

questions.q: Green amniotic fluid indicates meconium staining, which is classically seen in fetal distress, breech or transverse lie presentations, and:
questions.exp: Green staining is caused by meconium passage due to fetal distress, breech/transverse lie, or intrauterine Listeria infection. (Book p296)

questions.q: A golden-yellow coloration of amniotic fluid on amniocentesis is pathognomonic of excessive bilirubin accumulation due to:
opts: Rh isoimmunization / hemolytic disease of the fetus
Fetal duodenal atresia with bile reflux
Premature placental separation with lysed blood
questions.exp: Golden-yellow amniotic fluid is due to bilirubin pigments released during severe fetal hemolysis in Rh incompatibility. (Book p296)

questions.q: Match the abnormal amniotic fluid appearance with its correct underlying clinical condition:
opts: Dark red (port-wine): Concealed abruption; Tobacco-juice (dark brown): Intrauterine fetal death; Saffron: Post-term pregnancy
Dark red: Rh incompatibility; Tobacco-juice: Normal term; Saffron: Listeria infection
Dark red: Ectopic pregnancy; Tobacco-juice: Duodenal atresia; Saffron: Hydatidiform mole
Dark red: Meconium staining; Tobacco-juice: Abruptio; Saffron: Normal preterm
questions.exp: Dark red (port-wine) indicates concealed abruption, tobacco-juice (dark brown) indicates IUFD, and saffron indicates post-term dysmaturity. (Book p296)

questions.q: The clinical investigation of choice (IOC) for the quantitative assessment of amniotic fluid volume is:
questions.exp: Ultrasound is the non-invasive investigation of choice for measuring amniotic fluid parameters. (Book p296)

questions.q: The Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) is calculated by ultrasound as the sum total of the largest vertical pocket of fluid in:
opts: All four quadrants of the maternal abdomen (RUQ + LUQ + RLQ + LLQ)
The right and left upper quadrants only
A single deepest vertical pocket across the entire uterus
The retroplacental space and lower uterine segment
questions.exp: AFI is calculated by summing the deepest vertical pocket in each of the 4 abdominal quadrants (AFI = a + b + c + d). (Book p296)

questions.q: What is the normal physiological reference range for the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) in a singleton pregnancy?
questions.exp: The normal range for AFI is 5–24 cm; values <5 cm define oligohydramnios, and ≥25 cm define polyhydramnios. (Book p296)

questions.q: By definition, oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios are diagnosed when the AFI values are respectively:
opts: Oligohydramnios below 5 cm, and polyhydramnios at 25 cm or more
Oligohydramnios below 2 cm, and polyhydramnios above 8 cm
Oligohydramnios below 10 cm, and polyhydramnios at 35 cm or more
Oligohydramnios below 1 cm, and polyhydramnios at 15 cm or more
questions.exp: By amniotic fluid index, oligohydramnios is below 5 cm and polyhydramnios is 25 cm or more; the 2 cm and 8 cm values belong to the deepest pocket method. (Book p296)

questions.q: A major technical clinical limitation of using the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI) is that it:
opts: Cannot be accurately utilized in twin or multiple gestations
Exposes the fetus to excessive ionizing radiation
Requires invasive needle puncture of the amniotic sac
Can only be measured after 37 completed weeks of pregnancy
questions.exp: AFI cannot be used in multifetal pregnancies because the quadrants overlap both sacs; SDP must be used instead. (Book p296)

questions.q: A 34-year-old at 37 weeks has an amniotic fluid index of 4.2 cm with a single deepest vertical pocket of 3.1 cm. How should this scan be reported, and what follows?
opts: Oligohydramnios by AFI, though the deepest pocket is still adequate — look for rupture and monitor
Normal study, because both the AFI and the deepest vertical pocket are within normal limits
Polyhydramnios, because the AFI is above the 95th centile for gestational age
Severe oligohydramnios by both criteria, so immediate caesarean delivery is indicated
questions.exp: AFI at or below 5 cm is oligohydramnios, while a deepest pocket of 3.1 cm is still above the 2 cm threshold — the two methods disagree and must both be reported. (Book p296)

questions.q: What is the normal reference range for the Single Deepest Pocket (SDP) / Maximum Vertical Pocket (MVP) on ultrasound?
questions.exp: Normal SDP is 2–8 cm; an SDP <2 cm defines oligohydramnios, and >8 cm defines polyhydramnios. (Book p297)

questions.q: What are the key clinical advantages of measuring the Single Deepest Pocket (SDP) over the Amniotic Fluid Index (AFI)?
opts: It is more sensitive than AFI and can be reliably used in twin pregnancies
It provides a direct biochemical analysis of fetal hemoglobin
It measures maternal renal blood flow simultaneously
It can diagnose fetal neural tube defects without imaging
questions.exp: SDP is more sensitive than AFI, avoids overdiagnosis of oligohydramnios, and is valid in twin gestations. (Book p297)

questions.q: What is the most common etiology for mild polyhydramnios and mild oligohydramnios, respectively?
questions.exp: Mild cases of both polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios are most commonly idiopathic in origin. (Book p297)

questions.q: In severe polyhydramnios, what represents the single most common category of underlying etiologies?
opts: Gross congenital anomalies (Gastrointestinal tract obstructions > Neural tube defects)
questions.exp: Severe polyhydramnios is most commonly caused by gross congenital anomalies, with GIT defects (atresias) outnumbering NTDs. (Book p297)

questions.q: What is the leading cause of severe oligohydramnios diagnosed in the second trimester?
opts: Fetal renal anomalies (e.g., bilateral renal agenesis, PUV)
questions.exp: Severe oligohydramnios is most commonly due to fetal renal malformations impairing fetal urine production. (Book p297)

questions.q: The pathophysiological mechanism causing marked polyhydramnios in poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus is:
opts: Maternal hyperglycemia causing fetal hyperglycemia, which induces fetal osmotic polyuria
Impaired fetal swallowing due to cleft palate
Excessive transudation across fetal skin after 25 weeks
Placental hypoplasia with decreased fluid clearance
questions.exp: Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, driving fetal osmotic diuresis and massive polyuria into the amniotic sac. (Book p297)

questions.q: All of the following are causes of polyhydramnios EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Renal agenesis removes fetal urine output and causes oligohydramnios; obstruction, impaired swallowing and fetal polyuria cause polyhydramnios. (Book p297)

questions.q: Which of the following fetal malformations causes polyhydramnios specifically by impairing the fetal swallowing mechanism?
opts: Esophageal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula, and duodenal atresia
Posterior urethral valves and prune belly syndrome
Bilateral renal agenesis and multicystic kidney
Fetal coarctation of the aorta and tetralogy of Fallot
questions.exp: Swallowing defects preventing amniotic clearance include esophageal atresia, TEF, duodenal atresia, and cleft lip/palate. (Book p298)

questions.q: Chronologically, the most common cause of oligohydramnios in the second trimester vs the third trimester is:
opts: T2: Fetal renal anomalies; T3: Uteroplacental insufficiency (UPI) or PROM
T2: Gestational diabetes; T3: Fetal anemia
T2: Fetal swallowing defects; T3: Rh isoimmunization
questions.exp: In the 2nd trimester, fetal renal anomalies are the leading cause; in the 3rd trimester, UPI/IUGR and PROM predominate. (Book p298)

questions.q: In every patient diagnosed with oligohydramnios, what essential initial clinical step must be performed to exclude membrane rupture?
opts: Sterile speculum (P/S) examination to inspect for amniotic pooling and rule out PROM
Immediate digital vaginal examination with Bishop scoring
questions.exp: A sterile speculum examination must be performed in all oligohydramnios cases to rule out premature rupture of membranes (PROM). (Book p298)

questions.q: Which clinical entity can present with both oligohydramnios and polyhydramnios in the same pregnancy?
opts: Twin-to-Twin Transfusion Syndrome (TTTS: oligohydramnios in donor, polyhydramnios in recipient)
Fetal anencephaly in a singleton gestation
Bilateral renal agenesis in a singleton gestation
questions.exp: TTTS classically produces polyhydramnios in the recipient twin and severe oligohydramnios in the donor twin. (Book p298)

questions.q: In high-risk pregnancies complicated by significant amniotic fluid disorders, antepartum surveillance initiates at 28 weeks and includes:
opts: Weekly NST, weekly Biophysical Profile (BPP), and fetal growth USG every 3 weeks
Daily oxytocin challenge tests and daily amniocentesis
Monthly urine pregnancy testing and pelvic X-ray
questions.exp: Surveillance starts at 28 weeks with weekly NST, weekly biophysical score, and ultrasound for fetal growth every 3 weeks. (Book p299)

questions.q: What is the recommended gestational age for delivery by induction of labor in uncomplicated vs complicated amniotic fluid disorders?
questions.exp: Labor induction is scheduled at 39 completed weeks for uncomplicated cases and at 37 weeks for complicated disorders. (Book p299)

questions.q: Severe, prolonged oligohydramnios present early in pregnancy (first or early second trimester) is clinically most devastating because it causes:
opts: Pulmonary hypoplasia, the most lethal complication, and limb contractures
Duodenal atresia together with macroglossia in the newborn
A complete hydatidiform mole developing in the uterus
Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus before delivery
questions.exp: Severe early oligohydramnios is devastating because it causes pulmonary hypoplasia, the most lethal complication, and severe limb reduction contractures. (Book p299)

questions.q: In late pregnancy and active labor, oligohydramnios predisposes the fetus to which cardiotocographic (CTG) abnormality due to loss of fluid cushioning?
opts: Repetitive variable decelerations due to umbilical cord compression
Late decelerations occurring only after complete delivery
questions.exp: Loss of amniotic cushioning leads to umbilical cord compression, presenting on CTG as repetitive variable decelerations. (Book p299)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about oligohydramnios is TRUE?
opts: Potter sequence follows prolonged severe oligohydramnios beginning before about 22-24 weeks
Amniotic band syndrome is caused by oligohydramnios and is prevented by amnioinfusion
An amniotic fluid index of 8 cm is diagnostic of oligohydramnios in the third trimester
Isolated oligohydramnios at term is by itself an indication for immediate caesarean delivery
questions.exp: Only early, severe, prolonged oligohydramnios causes pulmonary hypoplasia with Potter facies and limb deformities; bands are a separate amnion-rupture problem. (Book p299)

questions.q: What constitutes the conservative mainstay of management for antenatal oligohydramnios?
opts: Strict bed rest in maternal left lateral position and aggressive maternal hydration
questions.exp: Mainstay conservative management includes bed rest in the left lateral position to optimize uterine perfusion and oral/IV hydration. (Book p300)

questions.q: Amnio-infusion of warm normal saline is specifically indicated and performed during active labor for:
opts: Persistent, severe variable decelerations due to cord compression
Antenatal treatment of pulmonary hypoplasia at 20 weeks
Preventing postpartum hemorrhage in twin pregnancy
questions.exp: Amnio-infusion with normal saline is indicated during active labor to alleviate persistent variable decelerations caused by cord compression. (Book p300)

questions.q: In uteroplacental insufficiency (UPI), the fetal 'brain-sparing effect' leads to oligohydramnios through which sequence?
opts: Cardiac output is preferentially shunted to the brain → Renal blood flow falls → GFR drops → Oliguria → Oligohydramnios
Blood is shunted to kidneys → Excessive urination → Bladder rupture
Renal vessels dilate → Glomerular filtration surges → Polyhydramnios
Systemic vasoconstriction causes pulmonary edema and amniotic fluid reabsorption
questions.exp: In UPI, blood is shunted to vital brain tissue, reducing renal perfusion; diminished GFR produces fetal oliguria and oligohydramnios. (Book p300)

questions.q: Potter's syndrome is primary bilateral renal agenesis with pulmonary hypoplasia and flat facies, whereas Potter's sequence refers to:
opts: The identical constellation of deformities resulting secondarily from any chronic severe oligohydramnios
The association of duodenal atresia with Down syndrome
Placental chorangioma combined with fetal hydrops
questions.exp: Potter's sequence describes the classic phenotypic triad arising secondary to any cause of severe oligohydramnios (such as PROM or PUV). (Book p300)

questions.q: Amniotic Band Syndrome (Streeter's syndrome) occurs when early rupture of the amnion produces loose fibrous strands that:
opts: Wrap tightly around fetal digits or extremities, forming constriction rings and causing amputations
Infiltrate the maternal myometrium to cause placenta percreta
Cross the internal os to cause vasa previa
Stimulate excessive fetal swallowing and severe polyhydramnios
questions.exp: Amniotic bands wrap tightly around fetal digits or limbs, producing deep constriction rings, distal digital hypoplasia, or amputation. (Book p300)

questions.q: In distinguishing limb reduction deformities, distal digital hypoplasia/amputation is characteristic of amniotic band syndrome and phenytoin, whereas proximal long-bone phocomelia is pathognomonic of:
questions.exp: Proximal limb reduction (phocomelia/seal limbs) is caused by thalidomide, whereas distal digital amputations occur in amniotic band syndrome. (Book p301)

questions.q: In severe symptomatic polyhydramnios (SDP ≥10 cm or AFI ≥35 cm) with maternal respiratory distress, therapeutic amnioreduction should remove:
opts: A maximum of 1.5 to 2.0 Liters slowly
Up to 5 Liters rapidly within 10 minutes
All fluid until the SDP measures <1 cm
questions.exp: Amnioreduction should slowly remove a maximum of 1.5–2.0 L to avoid abruptio placentae from rapid uterine decompression. (Book p301)

questions.q: When uterine irritability complicates symptomatic polyhydramnios, the recommended tocolytic regimens according to gestational age are:
opts: <32 weeks: Indomethacin; 32–34 weeks: Nifedipine; ≥34 weeks: Tocolytics not given
At all gestational ages: Indomethacin exclusively
Only intravenous magnesium sulfate throughout the third trimester
questions.exp: Indomethacin is used before 32 weeks, nifedipine is given from 32–34 weeks, and tocolytics are avoided at ≥34 weeks. (Book p301)

questions.q: In a patient in labor with marked polyhydramnios, artificial rupture of membranes (ARM) is strictly contraindicated because sudden gush of fluid precipitates:
opts: Umbilical cord prolapse and abruptio placentae
questions.exp: ARM is contraindicated in polyhydramnios because rapid decompression risks catastrophic umbilical cord prolapse and placental abruption. (Book p301)

questions.q: Overdistension of the uterus in severe polyhydramnios increases maternal and obstetric risks of:
opts: Preterm labor, unstable lie, placental abruption, and uterine atony PPH
Complete congenital heart block and Ebstein anomaly
questions.exp: Polyhydramnios predisposes to preterm labor, cord prolapse, abruptio placentae, malpresentation, and postpartum uterine atony. (Book p301)

questions.q: On fetal pelvic ultrasound, the classic 'keyhole sign' consisting of a distended bladder and dilated proximal posterior urethra is diagnostic of:
opts: Posterior urethral valves (PUV) causing severe oligohydramnios
Bilateral renal agenesis with empty bladder
questions.exp: The keyhole sign represents a distended bladder and dilated posterior urethra in male fetuses with PUV, producing severe oligohydramnios. (Book p301)

questions.q: The classic sonographic 'double bubble sign' on fetal abdominal imaging represents a fluid-filled stomach and dilated duodenum pathognomonic of:
opts: Duodenal atresia, which is associated with polyhydramnios and Down syndrome
questions.exp: The double bubble sign represents duodenal atresia, which prevents fluid absorption causing polyhydramnios and is strongly tied to Down syndrome. (Book p301)

questions.q: Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV / clubfoot) occurring as a secondary deformation in late gestation is classically associated with:
opts: Prolonged severe oligohydramnios with uterine crowding and compression
Maternal exposure to thalidomide in the third trimester
Excessive production of human placental lactogen
questions.exp: Prolonged severe oligohydramnios late in pregnancy restricts fetal movements and compresses extremities, leading to CTEV (clubfoot). (Book p301)

questions.q: Fill up: In severe polyhydramnios, amnioreduction removes fluid at about ______ mL per hour, and the drug used to reduce fetal urine output is ______.
questions.exp: Slow decompression at about 500 mL/hour limits abruption and preterm labour, and indomethacin reduces fetal urine output (with ductal constriction as the caveat). (Book p301)

units.title: Primordial Germ Cells & Sex Differentiation
units.guide: Gametogenesis starts with primordial germ cells arising from the epiblast and ectoderm. These bipotent cells differentiate into spermatogonia when the SRY gene on chromosome Y is present, or into oogonia when it is absent. The SRY locus sits on the distal end of the short arm of chromosome Y.

units.title: Spermatogenesis & Seminiferous Tubules
units.guide: Spermatogenesis initiates at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Type A spermatogonia maintain the stem pool while Type B spermatogonia enter meiosis, yielding 16 primary spermatocytes, which divide into secondary spermatocytes and then 64 spermatids. Spermiogenesis remodels round spermatids into spermatozoa without any cell division.

units.title: Sperm Structure, Maturation & Lifespan
units.guide: A mature spermatozoon measures 50–60 µm with an acrosome from the Golgi apparatus, a middle piece powerhouse packed with mitochondria, and a 9+2 axoneme from the centriole. Motility is acquired in the distal epididymis over 12–14 days, bringing total development time to 90 days. Once ejaculated, sperm reach the ampulla in 30 minutes and remain fertilisable for 48–72 hours.

units.title: Oogenesis & Follicular Dynamics
units.guide: Oogenesis begins in intrauterine life. Primary oocytes enter Meiosis I and arrest in the diplotene stage of prophase I (dictyate state) until the preovulatory LH surge triggers resumption. Meiosis II arrests at metaphase II and completes only upon fertilization. Follicles peak at 6–7 million at 5 months of fetal life, falling to 1–2 million at birth and 4–5 lakh at puberty.

units.title: Germ Cell Potency & Teratoma Origin
units.guide: Early zygotic blastomeres are totipotent, capable of building embryonic and extraembryonic structures, whereas germ cells are pluripotent. Primordial germ cells migrate from the epiblast across the yolk sac to the genital ridge; failure of migration with aberrant germ cell arrest along the midline produces teratomas.

units.title: Capacitation & Acrosome Reaction
units.guide: Capacitation occurs in the female tract over 6–8 hours (2 hours in vitro), conferring hypermotility. Sperm bind the ZP3 receptor on the zona pellucida and release hyaluronidase during the acrosome reaction. Fusion of the sperm head with the oolemma triggers the cortical and zona reactions to prevent polyspermy.

units.title: Fertilization, Cleavage & Tubal Transport
units.guide: Fertilization occurs in the ampulla on day 14 of a 28-day cycle. Cleavage yields a 2-cell embryo at 30 hours and a 16-cell morula that enters the uterine cavity on day 4 (cycle day 18), propelled by ciliated columnar cells and tubal peristalsis. On day 5, zona hatching frees the blastocyst; tubal immobility from Kartagener syndrome or progestin-only pills risks ectopic pregnancy.

units.title: Implantation Stages & Decidualisation
units.guide: Implantation occurs on day 6 post-fertilization (cycle day 20) during the receptive window from day 20 to 24. Apposition is mediated by selectins, adhesion by integrins, and penetration by matrix metalloproteinases. Progesterone drives decidualisation with marked stromal edema, creating the decidua basalis, capsularis, and parietalis, and giving the double decidual sign on ultrasound.

units.title: Blastocyst Differentiation & Trophoblast
units.guide: On day 8 post-fertilization, the blastocyst divides into the embryoblast and trophoblast. The inner cell mass generates all three definitive germ layers, while the trophoblast splits into syncytiotrophoblast—the placental hormone factory producing hCG and hPL—and cytotrophoblast. Extravillous trophoblasts remodel maternal spiral arteries, while chorion frondosum builds the fetal placenta.

units.title: Fetal Membranes & Yolk Sac
units.guide: Chorion arises from chorion laeve on day 8 as the outermost fetal membrane. Amnion forms on day 10 from embryonic ectoderm as an avascular, aneural inner membrane that supplies tensile strength. The yolk sac produces alpha-fetoprotein and serves as the initial site of hematopoiesis, while membrane rupture releases PGF2α to accelerate labor.

units.title: Preimplantation Genetic Testing & ART
units.guide: Preimplantation Genetic Testing screens embryos in assisted reproduction prior to transfer. It detects monogenic conditions such as sickle cell, cystic fibrosis, muscular dystrophy, and thalassemia, as well as aneuploidies and translocations. Polar body biopsy detects only maternal disorders and blastomere removal risks embryo injury, making trophectoderm biopsy at the blastocyst stage the gold standard.

units.title: Teratogenic Exposure & Radiation in Pregnancy
units.guide: Fetal growth periods from fertilization comprise the preimplantation period (0–2 weeks, governed by the all-or-none law), the embryonic period (3–8 weeks, the peak teratogenic phase of organogenesis), and the fetal period (≥9 weeks). Maximum permissible radiation is 5 Rads (0.05 Gy); doses >5 Rads cause microcephaly and IUGR, while ≥10 Rads trigger abortion. Ultrasound and non-contrast MRI are safe.

units.title: Teratogenic Drugs: Category X & Specific Malformations
units.guide: Category X medications carry proven fetal harm that far outweighs benefit, including androgens, DES, warfarin, ACE inhibitors, tetracyclines, thalidomide, lithium, and valproate. Alcohol causes smooth philtrum and cognitive impairment; phenytoin triggers fetal hydantoin syndrome; lithium induces Ebstein anomaly; thalidomide causes phocomelia; and warfarin causes chondrodysplasia punctata with stippled epiphyses.

units.title: Teratogenic Infections: TORCH & Congenital Syndromes
units.guide: CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss, classically presenting with periventricular calcifications. Toxoplasmosis shows chorioretinitis and diffuse intracranial calcifications, treated with spiramycin for mother and pyrimethamine-sulfadoxine for the fetus. Rubella causes cataracts, PDA, and SNHL; Parvovirus B19 attacks erythroid precursors causing hydrops; and maternal SLE causes complete congenital heart block.

units.title: Gross Placental Architecture & Placentomegaly
units.guide: The human placenta is discoid, deciduate, and hemochorial, weighing ~500 g at term with a 1:6 placenta-to-fetal weight ratio and equal weight at 17 weeks. Central thickness measures 2.5–4 cm; thickness >4 cm defines placentomegaly from diabetes, hydrops, or syphilis. The shiny fetal surface forms 4/5th of the placenta, while the dull red maternal surface forms 1/5th and is divided into 15–20 cotyledons.

units.title: Placental Villi Development & Trophoblastic Invasion
units.guide: The placental barrier separates maternal and fetal blood via syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, extraembryonic mesoderm, and fetal capillary endothelium. Primary villi form on day 13, secondary villi acquire a mesodermal core on day 16, and tertiary villi develop fetal vessels on day 17. Cytotrophoblast invades maternal spiral arteries, replacing their elastic coats to lower resistance and expand flow.

units.title: Placental Circulation & Cotyledon Anatomy
units.guide: Uteroplacental circulation in the intervillous space is established by day 12–13, carrying 500–700 ml/min at term out of a total uterine flow of 750 ml/min. Fetoplacental circulation in villi is established by day 17, flowing at 400 ml/min via the oxygenated umbilical vein and two deoxygenated umbilical arteries. Nitabuch's fibrinoid layer limits trophoblast penetration; its absence triggers placenta accreta.

units.title: Placental Respiration & Corpus Luteum Maintenance
units.guide: The placenta carries out respiratory, endocrine, nutritive, and excretory duties. Intervillous space blood matches umbilical vein oxygen saturation at 65–75% with a PO2 of 30–35 mm Hg. The corpus luteum peaks on day 22 and is rescued by syncytiotrophoblastic hCG from day 8 post-fertilization, sustaining progesterone until the luteal-placental shift at 8–10 weeks.

units.title: Placental Steroidogenesis & Labor Onset
units.guide: The placenta converts maternal cholesterol into progesterone to sustain pregnancy and quiet the myometrium. Lacking 17α-hydroxylase, the placenta depends on fetal adrenal DHEA-S for estrogen synthesis via placental sulfatase and aromatase. Labor onset follows functional progesterone withdrawal and an estrogen surge; absent fetal DHEA-S in anencephaly precipitates post-term pregnancy.

units.title: Human Placental Lactogen & hCG Endocrinology
units.guide: Human placental lactogen shares 96% homology with growth hormone, peaking at 36 weeks as an anti-insulin agent that spares glucose for the fetus. Human chorionic gonadotropin has a common alpha subunit and a unique beta subunit, peaking at 10 weeks (~100,000 IU/L) with a 36-hour half-life. The discriminatory zone is 2000 IU/L on TVS and 6500 IU/L on TAS.

units.title: Placental Morphological Anomalies & PAS
units.guide: Placenta accreta spectrum grades depth of villous attachment from accreta (superficial myometrium) to increta (deep invasion) and percreta (serosal penetration). Placenta bilobata features two equal parts with one cord, while placenta succenturiata has an accessory lobe connected by bridging vessels that risk retained lobe PPH. Extrachorial placentas form a ring, with circumvallate showing a raised rolled fold predisposing to abruption and IUGR.

units.title: Cord Insertion Anomalies, Vasa Previa & Apt Test
units.guide: Battledore placenta inserts marginally, while velamentous insertion attaches to membranes where vessels lack Wharton's jelly. When these membranous vessels cross the internal os, vasa previa results; rupture causes catastrophic fetal bleeding. Transvaginal color Doppler is the IOC, and an elective Cesarean is done at 34–37 weeks. The Apt alkali test stays pink with fetal HbF, confirming vasa previa over placenta previa.

units.title: Fetal Hematopoiesis & Placental Separation
units.guide: Hematopoiesis shifts from the yolk sac (<6 weeks) to the liver (6–30 weeks, producing HbF) and then the bone marrow (≥20 weeks, producing HbA). Newborn Hb is 16–18 g/dL with 75–90% HbF, falling to 1% by 6 months. In the third stage, placental separation cleaves along the decidual zona spongiosa via the Schultze mechanism (80%, central, shiny side first) or Duncan mechanism (20%, peripheral, dull side first).

units.title: Amniotic Fluid Dynamics & Color Signatures
units.guide: Amniotic fluid has a specific gravity of 1.008–1.010, pH of 7.2, and osmolarity of 260 mOsm/L, peaking at 1000 ml at 32–34 weeks before declining to 800 ml at term and 200 ml at 42 weeks. Fetal urination provides 1000 ml/day after 20 weeks, balanced by fetal swallowing. Amniotic fluid color signals pathology: green indicates meconium, golden indicates Rh incompatibility, dark red reflects abruptio, and tobacco juice marks IUFD.

units.title: Amniotic Fluid Assessment (AFI & SDP)
units.guide: Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for amniotic fluid assessment. The Amniotic Fluid Index sums the vertical diameter of the largest pocket across all four quadrants (normal 5–24 cm; <5 cm defines oligohydramnios and ≥25 cm defines polyhydramnios), though it cannot be used in twins. The Single Deepest Pocket measures 2–8 cm normally (<2 cm is oligohydramnios and >8 cm is polyhydramnios) and is valid in twin gestations.

units.title: Polyhydramnios & Oligohydramnios Etiology
units.guide: Mild polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios are most often idiopathic. Severe polyhydramnios stems from gross congenital anomalies—gastrointestinal obstructions like duodenal and esophageal atresia surpassing neural tube defects—as well as maternal diabetes causing fetal osmotic diuresis. Severe oligohydramnios is driven by fetal renal anomalies in the second trimester and uteroplacental insufficiency or PPROM in the third trimester, requiring a sterile speculum exam.

units.title: Fetal Monitoring, Oligohydramnios & Amniotic Bands
units.guide: Antepartum surveillance for fluid disorders starts at 28 weeks with weekly NST and BPP, and delivery at 39 weeks uncomplicated or 37 weeks complicated. Early oligohydramnios causes lethal pulmonary hypoplasia, while in labor it causes variable decelerations managed by left lateral rest and amnio-infusion. Amniotic band syndrome from early rupture creates constriction rings and digital amputations, distinct from thalidomide's proximal phocomelia.

units.title: Polyhydramnios Management & Classic Imaging Signs
units.guide: In severe symptomatic polyhydramnios, serial therapeutic amniocentesis slowly drains up to 1.5–2.0 L, with tocolytics used before 34 weeks (indomethacin before 32 weeks), while ARM is contraindicated. High-yield imaging features include the keyhole sign in posterior urethral valves (causing oligohydramnios), the double bubble sign in duodenal atresia (causing polyhydramnios and linked to Down syndrome), and CTEV clubfoot from oligohydramnios compression.
